topics.h: What if a river could talk to you? What advice would it give?
p: The lesson 'The Day the River Spoke' is about a girl, a river and her wish to learn. Here we read our own short story on the same idea.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when) and a plot (what happens).
The theme is the big idea or message of a story, such as courage or the right to learn.
Personification gives human actions to non-living things: 'The river whispered a secret.'
Clues in the text help us infer feelings: a girl who whispers her wish may feel shy or unsure.

ex.q: Read: Every morning, Meera sat on the steps by the river and watched children walk to school with their bags. "I want to read books too," she whispered. The river splashed softly and said, "Go on, little one. Even I keep moving forward." The next day, Meera asked her father if she could join the village school. How does Meera feel at first, and what helps her act?
st: Find the clue: she 'whispered' her wish, so she feels shy but longs to study.
Notice what changes: the river tells her to keep moving forward.
See the result: the next day she asks her father about school.
ex.a: At first Meera longs to study but is shy; the river's words give her courage, so she asks her father to let her join school.

topics.rl: When you look at a river, a tree or the moon and imagine it talking, you are using personification, just like poets and storytellers do.

rv.summary: This story is about Meera, who longs to go to school; the river's words give her courage to ask. Stories have characters, a setting and a plot, a theme, and may use personification.
focus: Identify the characters, setting and plot of a short story
Find the theme (the big idea or message)
Spot personification and infer feelings from clues
remember: Setting = where and when; plot = what happens
Theme = the big idea or message of a story
Personification = giving human actions to non-living things, e.g. 'The river whispered a secret.'
traps: Don't confuse the theme with the main character's name
A talking river is personification, not a simile
Infer feelings from clues like whispering, not from guesses

topics.h: In 1848, Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule started a school for girls in Pune, when very few girls in India went to school.
p: Education means learning and growing by reading, thinking and asking questions.
When girls study, they can follow their dreams, earn a living and help their families and villages.
India's Right to Education Act (2009) gives every child aged 6 to 14 the right to free and compulsory schooling.
Word family: educate (verb), education (noun), educated (adjective), educator (a person who teaches).
Literate means able to read and write; its opposite is illiterate.

ex.q: Read: Ritu's grandmother never went to school. Now Ritu teaches her the letters on bus boards, and Nani proudly reads out the name of their town. What does this show?
st: Ritu learned at school.
She shares her learning with her grandmother.
Nani learns to read even when she is old.
ex.a: Learning can happen at any age, and an educated girl can spread her learning to her whole family.

topics.rl: Look around: girls and women work as doctors, pilots, scientists, teachers and police officers — education opened those doors.

rv.summary: Education means learning by reading, thinking and asking questions. When girls study they can follow their dreams and help their families, and India's Right to Education Act gives every child aged 6 to 14 free schooling.
focus: Know the meaning of literate, illiterate and the education word family
Know the Right to Education Act and its age group
Explain why education for girls matters, with examples
remember: Right to Education Act (2009): free and compulsory schooling for children aged 6 to 14
educate (verb), education (noun), educated (adjective), educator (person)
Literate = able to read and write; opposite: illiterate
Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule started a girls' school in Pune in 1848
traps: Don't confuse literate with literal or literature
The opposite of literate is illiterate, not unliterate
'Educated' describes a person; 'education' is the noun

topics.h: The words river, Narmada, flock and hope are all nouns — but each is a different kind!
p: A noun is a naming word for a person, place, animal, thing or idea.
Common noun: a general name — girl, river, school.
Proper noun: a special name that begins with a capital letter — Meera, Narmada, Pune, Diwali.
Collective noun: a name for a group — a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a bunch of keys.
Abstract noun: a quality, feeling or idea you cannot touch — courage, honesty, knowledge, friendship.

ex.q: Find the nouns and their kinds: 'A class of girls showed great courage on the banks of the Ganga.'
st: 'class' names a group → collective noun
'girls' and 'banks' are general names → common nouns
'courage' is a quality we cannot touch → abstract noun
'Ganga' is a special name with a capital letter → proper noun
ex.a: class (collective), girls and banks (common), courage (abstract), Ganga (proper)

topics.rl: Shop signs, maps and your school ID card are full of proper nouns — that's why they begin with capital letters.

rv.summary: A noun is a naming word. Common nouns are general names, proper nouns are special names with capitals, collective nouns name groups, and abstract nouns name qualities, feelings or ideas.
focus: Sort nouns into common, proper, collective and abstract
Use the correct collective noun for a group
Form abstract nouns from adjectives and use capital letters for proper nouns
remember: Proper nouns begin with a capital letter: Meera, Kaveri, Pune, December
Collective nouns: a herd of elephants, a flock of birds, a school of fish, a pack of wolves
Abstract nouns: courage, honesty, kindness, bravery
traps: Don't write proper nouns like city or month names with small letters
Bravely is an adverb; the noun is bravery
The collective noun is the group word (herd), not the animals

topics.h: Did you know that most good things — riding a cycle, swimming, writing neatly — took many tries before they worked?
p: The poem 'Try Again' encourages us to keep trying after we fail. Here is our own poem on the same idea.
A poem is written in lines; a group of lines is called a stanza.
Rhyming words end with the same sound: two/do, tail/fail, say/way.
The rhyme scheme uses letters: lines that rhyme get the same letter, e.g. aabb.
Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult.

ex.q: Read: My kite fell down, it tore in two, / I sighed, "Now what am I to do?" / I tied the string, I fixed the tail, / I tried again — this time, no fail! / If once you slip, then rise and say, / "I'll try again, a better way." What is the rhyme scheme, and what is the message?
st: two/do rhyme → a a
tail/fail rhyme → b b
say/way rhyme → c c
The child fixes the kite and tries again instead of giving up.
ex.a: The rhyme scheme is aabbcc; the message is: when you fail, rise and try again in a better way.

topics.rl: Sports stars, scientists and even your favourite cricketers failed many times before they succeeded. They persevered.

rv.summary: This poem tells us to keep trying after we fail, just like a child who fixes a torn kite and flies it again. Poems are written in lines and stanzas, often with rhyming words that form a rhyme scheme.
focus: Find rhyming words and write the rhyme scheme (e.g. aabb)
Know the terms line, stanza and refrain
State the message of a poem on perseverance
remember: Rhyming words end with the same sound: two/do, tail/fail
Lines that rhyme get the same letter in the rhyme scheme
Perseverance = continuing to try even when something is difficult
'If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.'
traps: Don't call a group of lines in a poem a paragraph; it is a stanza
A refrain is a repeated line, not the rhyme scheme
In this poem 'slip' means fail once, not literally slipping

topics.t: Never give up: words of courage
topics.h: 'Give up', 'carry on', 'keep on' — tiny words like 'up' and 'on' completely change the meaning of a verb!
p: 'Give up' is a phrasal verb meaning 'stop trying'; 'carry on' and 'keep on' mean 'continue'.
Synonyms have similar meanings: determined, resolute, firm.
Antonyms are opposites; many are made with prefixes: un-, dis-, im-, in-, ir-, il-.
We often use im- before b, m, p (impossible, impatient), ir- before r (irregular) and il- before l (illegal).
Persistent means continuing firmly, never stopping trying.

ex.q: Change these words to their opposites: possible, patient, regular, legal.
st: possible starts with p → impossible
patient starts with p → impatient
regular starts with r → irregular
legal starts with l → illegal
ex.a: impossible, impatient, irregular, illegal

topics.rl: Coaches, teachers and parents say 'Don't give up!' and 'Keep it up!' — now you know these are phrasal verbs.

rv.summary: Words of courage include phrasal verbs like 'give up' (stop trying) and 'carry on' (continue), synonyms like determined and resolute, and antonyms often made with prefixes such as im-, ir- and il-.
focus: Know the meanings of give up, carry on and keep on
Find synonyms and antonyms of words about courage
Choose the right prefix for an opposite: im-, ir-, il-, un-, dis-, in-
remember: im- before b, m, p: impossible, impatient
ir- before r: irregular; il- before l: illegal
Determined = resolute; persistent = continuing firmly, never stopping trying
traps: 'Give up' means stop trying, not pick something up
Don't write 'unpatient' or 'imregular'
The opposite of success is failure, not effort

topics.h: Helen Keller could not see or hear — yet she wrote books, travelled the world and earned a college degree!
p: Helen Keller (1880–1968) was an American writer. An illness took away her sight and hearing when she was about 19 months old.

Her teacher Anne Sullivan taught her words by spelling them into her hand. Her big breakthrough came when she understood that the letters spelled into her palm meant the 'water' pouring over her other hand.
In 1904 she graduated from Radcliffe College — the first deafblind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree.
'Three Days to See' is an essay in which she imagines what she would look at if she could see for three days.
An essay is a short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's thoughts and feelings.

ex.q: Read this short piece in the spirit of the essay: "If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face. Then I would gaze at a marigold garland, bright orange and gold. At night I would lie on the roof and count the stars until I fell asleep." What is the writer asking us to value?
st: List what the writer wants to see: a loved face, colours, the stars.
These are everyday sights we often ignore.
So the message is to notice and treasure what we can see.
ex.a: To treasure the ordinary sights around us — faces, colours and the night sky — instead of taking them for granted.

topics.rl: Next time you see a sunset or your friend's smile, pause for a moment and really look — that is what Helen Keller asked people to do.

rv.summary: Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing as a baby, learned words from Anne Sullivan, and became the first deafblind person to earn a BA. In her essay 'Three Days to See' she asks us to value our senses.
focus: Recall key facts about Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan
Know what an essay is
State the message of 'Three Days to See'
remember: Helen Keller (1880–1968) lost sight and hearing after an illness at about 19 months
Anne Sullivan taught her by spelling words into her hand ('water' was her breakthrough)
1904: graduated from Radcliffe College, first deafblind person to earn a BA
An essay is a short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's thoughts
traps: 'Three Days to See' is an essay, not a poem or play
To take something for granted means not valuing it, not thanking for it
She lost her senses through illness, not an accident

topics.h: Your nose can recognise the smell of hot jalebis even before you see the shop!
p: We have five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue) and touch (skin).
Sensory words help readers imagine: glittering (sight), crackling (sound), fragrant (smell), tangy (taste), velvety (touch).
Braille is a reading system of raised dots invented by Louis Braille of France. Each Braille cell has six dot positions.
People who are deaf may use sign language; India has its own Indian Sign Language (ISL).
Melodious means sweet-sounding; fragrant means sweet-smelling.

ex.q: Which senses are used in: 'The sizzling jalebis smelled sweet and felt sticky in my fingers'?
st: 'sizzling' is a sound → hearing
'smelled sweet' → smell
'felt sticky' → touch
ex.a: Hearing, smell and touch

topics.rl: Lifts, ATMs and some medicine boxes have Braille dots so that people who cannot see can use them.

rv.summary: We have five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Sensory words help readers imagine, and people who cannot see or hear use Braille and sign language.
focus: Match sensory words to the correct sense
Know the sense organ for each sense
Know facts about Braille and Indian Sign Language
remember: Sight–eyes, hearing–ears, smell–nose, taste–tongue, touch–skin
Braille was invented by Louis Braille of France; each cell has 6 dot positions
Fragrant = sweet-smelling; melodious = sweet-sounding
India has its own Indian Sign Language (ISL)
traps: Fragrant is about smell, not taste
Rustling is a sound word, not a touch word
A Braille cell has 6 dot positions, not 8

topics.h: Good, better, best! Some adjectives change completely when we compare.
p: Positive degree describes one thing: tall, beautiful.
Comparative degree compares two things and is often followed by 'than': taller, more beautiful.
Superlative degree compares three or more and usually takes 'the': the tallest, the most beautiful.
Long adjectives use more/most: more precious, most precious.
Irregular forms: good–better–best, bad–worse–worst, many–more–most, little–less–least. Spelling: big–bigger, happy–happier.

ex.q: Complete: 'The Taj Mahal looks ___ (beautiful) at sunrise than at noon.'
st: Two times are compared (sunrise and noon), and 'than' follows → comparative.
'Beautiful' is a long word, so we use 'more'.
ex.a: more beautiful

topics.rl: Shops say 'Bigger! Better! Best!' and sports reporters say 'the fastest bowler' — that's degrees of comparison.

rv.summary: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (one thing), comparative (two things, often with 'than') and superlative (three or more, usually with 'the'). Long adjectives use more/most and some forms are irregular.
focus: Form comparatives and superlatives with -er/-est or more/most
Learn irregular forms and spelling changes
Choose the right degree from clues like 'than', 'the' and 'of all'
remember: good–better–best; bad–worse–worst; many–more–most; little–less–least
big → bigger (double the last letter); happy → happier (y to i)
Comparative + than; the + superlative
traps: Don't use two comparatives together, e.g. 'more happier'
Don't say 'the most high'; say 'the highest'
Use the comparative, not the superlative, when only two things are compared

topics.h: Imagine asking a cat why it knocks things off the table — and getting an answer!
p: Doctor Dolittle is a character created by the English writer Hugh Lofting. He is a doctor who learns to talk with animals.
In the stories, his parrot Polynesia teaches him the language of animals, and he becomes a doctor for animals.
A doctor who treats animals is called a veterinarian, or vet.
Real animals communicate with sounds, movements and smells — honeybees even do a 'waggle dance' to show where flowers are.
Our own story below imagines a clinic where a bird helps a doctor understand animals.

ex.q: Read: Dr Mehta's clinic in Pune was full of patients — but none of them were people! A goat with a sore hoof bleated, "Ma-a-a, my foot hurts!" Mynah, the clinic's chatty bird, flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "Thank you, Mynah," smiled Dr Mehta. "What would I do without my translator?" Why does Dr Mehta call Mynah his 'translator'?
st: A translator changes words from one language into another.
The goat speaks in animal language; Mynah explains it to the doctor.
So Mynah does a translator's job.
ex.a: Because Mynah turns the animals' language into words the doctor can understand.

topics.rl: Vets at animal hospitals and gaushalas read animals' body language — a limping goat or a cat that won't eat tells them something is wrong.

rv.summary: Doctor Dolittle, created by Hugh Lofting, learns animal language from his parrot Polynesia and becomes a doctor for animals. Our story imagines a vet whose mynah acts as a translator, while real animals communicate with sounds, movements and smells.
focus: Recall facts about Doctor Dolittle and Hugh Lofting
Know animal sound words and the word 'veterinarian'
Tell real animal communication from fantasy, and see what makes a line funny
remember: Doctor Dolittle was created by Hugh Lofting; Polynesia the parrot taught him animal language
A vet (veterinarian) treats animals
Goats bleat, horses neigh, elephants trumpet, owls hoot
Honeybees do a 'waggle dance' to show where flowers are
traps: Polynesia is a parrot, not the dog (Jip) or monkey (Chee-Chee)
A paediatrician treats children, not animals
To translate means to change words into another language, not to carry

topics.h: A crocodile booking a train ticket to visit the dentist? That's imagination at work!
p: Fantasy describes things that cannot happen in real life, like talking animals or flying carpets.
Realistic writing describes things that could really happen.
Humour comes from surprise, silly situations, funny talk and exaggeration.
Exaggeration (hyperbole) makes something sound much bigger than it is: 'I've told you a million times!'
Word family: imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginary and imaginative (adjectives).

ex.q: Is this fantasy or real, and why is it funny? 'The crocodile booked a train ticket to Chennai to see the dentist.'
st: Crocodiles cannot book tickets → fantasy.
A huge-toothed crocodile worried about its teeth is a silly surprise.
ex.a: It is fantasy, and it is funny because of the silly, surprising situation.

topics.rl: Cartoons, comics and funny ads on TV use talking animals and exaggeration to make us laugh.

rv.summary: Fantasy describes things that cannot really happen, while realistic writing describes things that could. Writers create humour with surprise, silly situations and exaggeration (hyperbole).
focus: Tell fantasy sentences from realistic ones
Spot exaggeration and explain why a line is funny
Use the word family imagine, imagination, imaginary, imaginative
remember: Fantasy: talking animals, flying carpets; realistic: could really happen
Exaggeration (hyperbole): 'This bag weighs a ton!'
imagine (verb), imagination (noun), imaginary and imaginative (adjectives)
traps: Exaggeration is not a simile; there is no 'like' or 'as'
'Imaginary' means not real; it does not mean very large
Grave, solemn and stern mean serious; the opposite is funny

topics.h: Quotation marks are like a speech bubble in a comic — they hold a speaker's exact words.
p: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Mynah said, "The goat is hurt."
The spoken words begin with a capital letter, and a comma, full stop, question mark or exclamation mark comes before the closing quotation mark.
Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quotation marks, often using 'that': Mynah said that the goat was hurt.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said), the tense usually moves back: am/is → was, can → could, will → would, like → liked.
Pronouns change to fit: Rohan said, "I am tired." → Rohan said that he was tired. Universal truths stay in the present tense.

ex.q: Change to reported speech: Rohan said, "I can help the goat."
st: Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
'I' (Rohan) becomes 'he'.
'can' moves back to 'could' because 'said' is past.
ex.a: Rohan said that he could help the goat.

topics.rl: News reports, comics and your diary use both — direct speech for exact words, reported speech to retell them.

rv.summary: Direct speech gives the exact words in quotation marks; reported speech tells what was said without them, usually with 'that'. After 'said', tenses usually move back and pronouns change, but universal truths stay in the present.
focus: Punctuate direct speech correctly
Change direct speech into reported speech
Apply tense and pronoun changes and the universal-truth rule
remember: Mynah said, "The goat is hurt." → Mynah said that the goat was hurt.
am/is → was, can → could, will → would, like → liked
Pronouns change: "I am tired." → he/she was tired
Question marks and full stops go inside the closing quotation marks
traps: Don't keep 'I' in reported speech when it refers to the speaker
Universal truths do not change tense: the Earth goes around the Sun
After could, use the base verb: could swim, not could swam

topics.h: Some poems are written just to make you giggle — and that's a serious skill!
p: 'A Funny Man' is a humorous poem about a person who does odd, funny things. Here is our own funny poem.
A humorous poem makes us laugh with silly people, odd actions and surprising rhymes.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem — the pattern of strong and weak sounds you can clap to.
Two lines next to each other that rhyme are called a rhyming couplet (rhyme scheme aabb).
Sound words like 'click-clack' are called onomatopoeia.

ex.q: Read: Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands, / And sang to the goats in the sugarcane lands. / He rode on a bullock cart, facing the back, / And laughed till his glasses went click-clack! What is the rhyme scheme, and what makes the poem funny?
st: hands/lands rhyme → aa; back/clack rhyme → bb
Funny actions: shoes on hands, singing to goats, riding facing backwards
ex.a: The rhyme scheme is aabb; the silly, upside-down actions of Uncle Bholu make it funny.

topics.rl: Funny rhymes are used in ads, birthday cards and school function skits because they are easy to remember.

rv.summary: A humorous poem makes us laugh with silly people, odd actions and surprising rhymes, like Uncle Bholu wearing shoes on his hands. Poems have rhythm, may use rhyming couplets and sound words called onomatopoeia.
focus: Explain what makes a line in a poem funny
Find rhyming words and the rhyme scheme (aabb, abab)
Identify couplets, rhythm and onomatopoeia
remember: Rhyming couplet = two lines next to each other that rhyme (aabb)
Rhythm = the beat or pattern of strong and weak sounds
Onomatopoeia = sound words like 'click-clack'
Humorous = funny
traps: Don't confuse a couplet with a refrain (a repeated line)
Alternating rhymes (sun, bed, fun, red) give abab, not aabb
Onomatopoeia is about sound, not giving human actions to things

topics.h: Malayalam is the name of a language — and it reads the same backwards!
p: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: sea/see, flour/flower, knight/night.
Alliteration repeats the same first sound in nearby words: 'Pinky's pet parrot picked papayas.'
Tongue twisters use alliteration to make saying them tricky and fun.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards: madam, level, noon, Malayalam.
A pun is a joke that plays on two meanings of a word or on words that sound alike.

ex.q: Explain the joke: 'Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tired!'
st: 'Two-tired' means having two tyres.
It sounds just like 'too tired' (very tired).
The joke plays on the two meanings.
ex.a: It is a pun: 'two-tired' (two tyres) sounds like 'too tired'.

topics.rl: Riddles in children's magazines, jokes on wrappers and ads on hoardings are full of puns and alliteration.

rv.summary: Word play includes homophones (same sound, different spelling and meaning), alliteration and tongue twisters (repeated first sounds), palindromes (same both ways) and puns (jokes on two meanings or sound-alike words).
focus: Pick the correct homophone for a sentence
Spot alliteration and palindromes
Explain how a pun works
remember: Homophones: sea/see, flour/flower, knight/night, week/weak
Alliteration: 'Pinky's pet parrot picked papayas.'
Palindromes: madam, level, noon, Malayalam
Pun: 'two-tired' sounds like 'too tired'
traps: Synonyms like big–large are not homophones
Don't mix up flour (for rotis) and flower (on a plant)
A palindrome must read the same backwards letter by letter

topics.h: A play is a story that comes alive — actors become the characters right in front of you!
p: 'Say the Right Thing' is a funny play about manners and choosing our words. Here is our own short scene.
A play is a story written to be acted on stage; it is told mostly through dialogue (what the characters say).
The speaker's name comes before each line, and the cast is the list of characters.
Stage directions, usually in brackets or italics, tell actors how to move or speak. They are not spoken aloud.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes. The people who watch are the audience.

ex.q: Read: (A busy kitchen. AMMA is rolling rotis. TINU runs in.) TINU: Amma, give me water! AMMA: (raising an eyebrow) Is that how we ask? TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water? AMMA: Of course, beta. (She hands him a glass.) Which parts are stage directions, and how is Tinu's second line different from his first?
st: Words in brackets, like '(raising an eyebrow)', are stage directions.
First line: an order — 'give me water!'
Second line: a polite request with 'may I' and 'please'.
ex.a: The bracketed parts are stage directions; Tinu's second line is polite because he uses 'May I please…'.

topics.rl: School annual-day plays, Ramlila performances and street plays (nukkad natak) all use dialogue and stage directions.

rv.summary: A play is a story written to be acted, told mostly through dialogue. Each line begins with the speaker's name, stage directions in brackets guide the actors, and plays are divided into acts and scenes watched by an audience.
focus: Tell dialogue from stage directions
Know the terms cast, audience, act and scene
Read a scene and explain how a character's words change
remember: Dialogue = conversation between characters
Stage directions (in brackets or italics) guide actors and are not spoken
Cast = list of characters; audience = people who watch
Plays are divided into acts and scenes
traps: Don't read stage directions aloud as dialogue
The cast acts; the audience watches
Plays have acts and scenes, not stanzas or chapters

topics.h: The same request can sound like a command or a kind question — it all depends on the words you choose!
p: Please, thank you, sorry and excuse me are polite words that make conversations kind.
Polite requests often begin with 'Could you…?', 'Would you…?' or 'May I…?'
'May I' asks for permission. 'Can' usually shows ability: 'Rani can swim.'
When someone thanks you, reply 'You're welcome.'
Our tone of voice and body language also show respect.

ex.q: Make this polite: 'Give me your pencil.'
st: Begin with a polite modal: 'Could you…'
Add 'please'.
Use a gentle verb like 'lend'.
ex.a: Could you please lend me your pencil?

topics.rl: At home, in shops, on the bus and in class, polite words make people happy to help you.

rv.summary: Polite words like please, thank you, sorry and excuse me make conversations kind. Polite requests begin with 'Could you', 'Would you' or 'May I'; 'may' asks permission while 'can' shows ability.
focus: Turn orders into polite requests
Choose the right polite word for a situation
Tell 'may' (permission) from 'can' (ability)
remember: Polite requests: Could you…? Would you…? May I…?
'May I come in?' asks permission; 'Rani can swim' shows ability
Reply to 'Thank you' with 'You're welcome'
Say 'Sorry' for a mistake and 'Excuse me' to get attention
traps: 'Give me…' is an order, not a polite request
Don't use 'can' when asking permission formally; use 'may'
Tone and body language matter as much as words

topics.h: If your teacher says 'Hold your horses!', don't look for horses in the classroom!
p: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
'It's raining cats and dogs' means it is raining heavily — no animals fall from the sky!
Taking an idiom literally (word for word) can cause funny misunderstandings — a common source of humour in plays.
Good communication means choosing words that the listener will understand.
Tone matters: the same words can sound kind or rude depending on how we say them.

ex.q: Dadi says, 'Hold your horses!' and Chintu looks around for horses. Why is this funny, and what did Dadi mean?
st: Chintu takes the words literally.
'Hold your horses' is an idiom.
It means 'wait' or 'be patient'.
ex.a: It's funny because Chintu takes the idiom literally; Dadi meant 'Wait, be patient.'

topics.rl: Cricket commentators, film dialogues and grandparents all love idioms — knowing them helps you understand people better.

rv.summary: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning differs from the separate words, like 'raining cats and dogs' for heavy rain. Taking idioms literally causes funny misunderstandings.
focus: Give the meanings of common idioms
Explain why a literal reading of an idiom is funny
Use idioms correctly in sentences
remember: A piece of cake = very easy; once in a blue moon = very rarely
Break the ice = start a friendly talk; let the cat out of the bag = tell a secret by mistake
Hold your horses = wait; under the weather = unwell; over the moon = very happy
Use your head = think carefully
traps: Don't take idioms word for word
'Under the weather' means unwell, not standing in the rain
'Over the moon' means very happy, not a space trip

topics.h: Every gadget you use — from a pencil sharpener to a mobile phone — began as someone's 'crazy' idea!
p: 'My Brother's Great Invention' is a lesson about a sibling who keeps creating things. Here is our own story on the theme.
To invent is to make something new that did not exist before.
To discover is to find something that already existed but was not known: C. V. Raman discovered the Raman effect in 1928.
Inventors are curious, creative and patient; each failure shows them how to improve.
Word family: invent (verb), invention (noun), inventor (person), inventive (adjective).

ex.q: Read: My brother Kunal tied an old umbrella, two spoons and a toy motor together. "Behold the Mango-Picker 3000!" he announced. The machine wobbled, buzzed and shook the branch — and one ripe mango dropped straight onto his head. Kunal rubbed his head and grinned. "Version two will have a basket," he said. What does 'Version two will have a basket' show about Kunal?
st: The machine shook the mango loose, but it fell on his head — a small failure.
Kunal grins instead of getting upset.
He already plans an improvement: a basket to catch the mango.
ex.a: He learns from his mistake and plans to improve his invention — he is creative and does not give up.

topics.rl: India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the day in 1928 when C. V. Raman announced his discovery.

rv.summary: To invent is to make something new; to discover is to find something that already existed. Inventors like Kunal are curious, creative and patient, learning from each failure, and C. V. Raman's 1928 discovery is honoured on National Science Day.
focus: Tell 'invent' from 'discover' in sentences
Use the word family invent, invention, inventor, inventive
Infer a character's qualities from what he says and does
remember: Invent = make something new; discover = find what already existed
invent (verb), invention (noun), inventor (person), inventive (adjective)
C. V. Raman discovered the Raman effect in 1928; National Science Day is 28 February
traps: Scientists discover a new frog; they do not invent it
An inventor is the person; an invention is the thing made
Failure is part of inventing; it shows how to improve

topics.h: One tiny mark — the apostrophe — tells you whether the robot belongs to one brother or to three!
p: Siblings are brothers and sisters. Friendly competition between them is called sibling rivalry.
To show that something belongs to one person, add 's: my brother's invention.
For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: my brothers' room (two or more brothers).
For a plural noun not ending in s, add 's: the children's toys, the women's team.
Its = belonging to it (The cat licked its paw). It's = it is (It's raining).

ex.q: I have one sister. Is it 'my sisters' bicycle' or 'my sister's bicycle'?
st: Only one sister owns the bicycle → singular noun.
For a singular noun we add 's.
ex.a: my sister's bicycle

topics.rl: Name boards like 'Sharma's Sweets' or 'Children's Park' use apostrophes to show who something belongs to.

rv.summary: Siblings are brothers and sisters. An apostrophe shows belonging: add 's for one owner, only ' for plurals ending in s, and 's for plurals like children. Its shows belonging; it's means it is.
focus: Use 's and s' correctly to show belonging
Choose between its and it's
Know family words like siblings, aunt and sibling rivalry
remember: One owner: my brother's invention
Plural ending in s: my brothers' room; plural not ending in s: the children's toys
Its = belonging to it; it's = it is
Sibling rivalry = competition between brothers and sisters
traps: Don't write 'childrens'' — children is already plural, so it is children's
Don't use it's for belonging
Three sisters share a room: sisters', not sister's

topics.h: Even a great inventor needs clear steps — or the machine ends up upside down!
p: Instructions tell how to make or do something, step by step.
They use imperative sentences — commands or requests that usually begin with a verb: 'Cut the paper.' The subject 'you' is understood.
Sequence words show order: first, next, then, after that, finally.
A list of materials (things needed) comes before the steps.
Other kinds of sentences: assertive (statement), interrogative (question) and exclamatory (strong feeling).

ex.q: Write instructions for making nimbu pani (lemonade).
st: Materials: a glass of water, one lemon, sugar, a pinch of salt.
First, squeeze the lemon into the water.
Next, add sugar and a pinch of salt.
Then stir well.
Finally, serve it cool.
ex.a: First squeeze the lemon, next add sugar and salt, then stir, and finally serve.

topics.rl: Recipe books, game rules, medicine labels and model kits all use imperative sentences and sequence words.

rv.summary: Instructions tell how to make or do something step by step. They list the materials first, use imperative sentences that begin with a verb, and use sequence words like first, next, then and finally.
focus: Write steps as imperative sentences starting with a verb
Use sequence words in order
Identify assertive, interrogative, imperative and exclamatory sentences
remember: Imperative: command or request, usually starting with a verb; the subject 'you' is understood
Sequence words: first, next, then, after that, finally
Materials (things needed) come before the steps
Assertive = statement; interrogative = question; exclamatory = strong feeling
traps: Begin a step with the base verb (Put), not 'Putting' or 'Puts'
'Please shut the door' is imperative, not interrogative
'Finally' begins the last step, not the first

topics.h: Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of TWO countries — India's and Bangladesh's!
p: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was a poet, writer, musician and painter from Bengal, lovingly called Gurudev.
In 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature — the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize.
He wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', India's national anthem.
He started a school at Santiniketan in West Bengal, which grew into Visva-Bharati University.
His poem 'Paper Boats' shows a child sending boats down a stream, dreaming they will reach faraway lands. Below is our own poem on that idea.

ex.q: Read: I fold my homework sheet into a boat, / And set it on the stream where raindrops float. / I draw a smiling sun in crayon blue — / Dear stranger, will this boat sail all the way to you? What does the child hope for?
st: The child sets the boat on a stream.
The child draws a smiling sun on it.
'Dear stranger' — the child hopes someone far away will find it.
ex.a: The child hopes the boat will travel far and reach a stranger in another place.

topics.rl: Every time you sing 'Jana Gana Mana' in the school assembly, you are singing Tagore's words.

rv.summary: Rabindranath Tagore (Gurudev) was a poet from Bengal who won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote 'Jana Gana Mana' and started a school at Santiniketan. In 'Paper Boats' a child sends boats downstream, hoping they reach faraway lands.
focus: Recall key facts about Tagore's life and work
Explain the child's hope in the paper-boat poem
Find rhyming words and the main feeling of the poem
remember: Tagore (1861–1941) won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, the first Asian Nobel winner
He wrote India's national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana'
Santiniketan (West Bengal) grew into Visva-Bharati University
traps: 'Vande Mataram' was written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, not Tagore
Tagore's Nobel was in Literature, not Peace
A stranger is someone you do not know

topics.h: 'My dreams are kites' — can a dream really be a kite? In a poem, it can!
p: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': 'The boat bobbed like a duck.'
A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The stream was a silver ribbon.'
Similes and metaphors paint pictures in the reader's mind.
Common similes: as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as light as a feather.
We use 'will' to talk about future dreams: 'One day I will become a pilot.'

ex.q: Simile or metaphor? (a) 'The paper boat floated like a leaf.' (b) 'Childhood is a garden of dreams.'
st: (a) uses 'like' → simile
(b) says childhood IS a garden, no 'like' or 'as' → metaphor
ex.a: (a) is a simile; (b) is a metaphor.

topics.rl: Film songs, poems and even everyday talk ('She's a star!') are full of similes and metaphors.

rv.summary: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor says one thing IS another. Both paint pictures in the reader's mind. We use 'will' to talk about future dreams.
focus: Tell similes from metaphors
Complete common similes
Use 'will' for future plans and dreams
remember: Simile: 'The boat bobbed like a duck.'
Metaphor: 'The stream was a silver ribbon.'
as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, as cool as a cucumber, as light as a feather, as white as snow
traps: A comparison with 'like' or 'as' is a simile, not a metaphor
Don't use past tense (did, was) for future dreams; use 'will'

topics.h: Before phones, travellers wrote letters — and a single letter could carry a whole journey inside it!
p: 'North, South, East, West' is a lesson made of letters written from different parts of India. Here we learn to write such letters.
An informal letter is written to family or friends in a warm, chatty style.
Parts of an informal letter: sender's address, date, salutation (Dear Anu,), body, closing (With love,) and name.
A formal letter (to a principal or an officer) uses 'Sir/Madam', a subject line and a closing like 'Yours sincerely'.
Travel letters describe places, food, weather, people and feelings. P.S. (postscript) adds a note after the letter ends.

ex.q: Read: Dear Anu, Greetings from Shillong! It rained three times today, and the hills wore a cap of clouds. We ate hot momos near the market. I wish you were here! With love, Tara. P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple! Find the salutation, the closing and the postscript.
st: 'Dear Anu,' greets the reader → salutation.
'With love, Tara' ends the letter → closing and name.
'P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple!' is added at the end → postscript.
ex.a: Salutation: 'Dear Anu,' — Closing: 'With love, Tara' — Postscript: 'P.S. I'm bringing you a pineapple!'

topics.rl: Emails and holiday messages follow the same idea: greet, share your news, close warmly.

rv.summary: Travel letters describe places, food, weather and feelings. An informal letter to family or friends has an address, date, salutation, body, warm closing and name; a formal letter uses Sir/Madam, a subject line and 'Yours sincerely'.
focus: Name the parts of an informal letter in order
Tell informal letters from formal ones
Read a travel letter and pick out details
remember: Order: sender's address, date, salutation, body, closing, name
Salutation: 'Dear Anu,'; informal closing: 'With love,'
Formal letters (to a principal): Sir/Madam, subject line, 'Yours sincerely'
P.S. (postscript) = a note added after the letter is finished
traps: Don't use 'Yours faithfully' in a letter to a friend
The salutation is the greeting, not the closing
The date goes near the top, below the address

topics.h: Travel from Ladakh to Kanyakumari and you'll pass snow, deserts, rainforests and beaches — all in one country!
p: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
North: Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh have the high Himalayan mountains.
South: Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka; Kanyakumari is at the southern tip of mainland India.
East and North-east: West Bengal, Odisha and Assam; Bihu is celebrated in Assam. West: Gujarat and Rajasthan; the Thar Desert lies mostly in Rajasthan.
Culture means a group's way of life — food, language, clothes, festivals, music and dance.

ex.q: Tara writes from Assam, Arjun from Kerala and Kiran from Rajasthan. Which direction of India is each in?
st: Assam is in the North-east.
Kerala is in the South.
Rajasthan is in the West (North-west).
ex.a: Tara — North-east, Arjun — South, Kiran — West

topics.rl: Indian railways connect all four directions; a long journey shows you new foods, languages and dances at every station.

rv.summary: India's regions have different landscapes and cultures: Himalayas in the north, Kanyakumari at the southern tip, Bihu in Assam, the Thar Desert in Rajasthan and Kathakali in Kerala. Culture is a group's whole way of life.
focus: Place states in the correct direction of India
Match festivals, dances and landmarks to states
Know the meaning of culture and opposite directions
remember: Sun rises in the east, sets in the west
Kanyakumari: southern tip of mainland India
Bihu: Assam; Kathakali: Kerala; Thar Desert: mostly Rajasthan
Opposite of north-east is south-west
traps: Gujarat is in the west, not the North-east
Culture is not just weather or population; it is a way of life

topics.h: Over the bridge, through the tunnel, along the river — tiny words guide every journey!
p: A preposition shows how a noun or pronoun is related to another word, often by place, direction or time.
Place: in, on, under, between, beside, near, behind, at.
Direction or movement: to, towards, into, across, along, through, up, down.
'In' shows position inside; 'into' shows movement from outside to inside.
'Between' is used for two people or things; 'among' for more than two.

ex.q: Fill the blanks: 'The ferry went ___ the river, and we walked ___ the bank to the temple.'
st: Going from one side to the other side → across
Moving beside the length of the bank → along
ex.a: across, along

topics.rl: Maps, signboards and GPS directions use prepositions: 'Turn left at the signal, go across the bridge.'

rv.summary: Prepositions show how a noun or pronoun relates to another word, often by place or direction. Use in/on/at/under/between for place and to/into/across/along/through for movement.
focus: Choose prepositions of place and direction
Tell in from into and between from among
Use at, in and through correctly
remember: Across = from one side to the other; along = beside the length of something
Into = movement from outside to inside; in = position inside
Between = two; among = more than two
At a point (at the bus stop); in a city (in Kolkata); through a tunnel
traps: Don't use 'between' for many people; use 'among'
Don't use 'in' for movement into a place; use 'into'

topics.h: What's waiting at the other end of a dark tunnel? Adventure stories keep you guessing!
p: 'The Tunnel' is an adventure story set around a railway tunnel in a forest. Here is our own short adventure.
An adventure story has excitement, a challenge or danger, and a character who shows courage.
Story elements: setting, characters, problem (conflict), climax (most exciting point) and resolution (how it ends).
Writers build suspense with short sentences, sound words and unanswered questions.
Courage does not mean feeling no fear — it means facing your fear.

ex.q: Read: The moment the train entered the tunnel, the whole compartment went black. Ishaan gripped the window bar. The wheels roared, and his heart drummed fast. He counted slowly — one, two, three… At twenty, a burst of green and gold light flooded in: paddy fields and a sparkling river. "That wasn't scary at all," he grinned. What is the problem, the climax and the resolution?
st: Problem: the dark tunnel makes Ishaan scared.
Climax: the roaring darkness while he counts.
Resolution: light floods in and he smiles — his fear is gone.
ex.a: Problem — fear of the dark tunnel; climax — the roaring dark while he counts; resolution — the bright fields appear and he grins.

topics.rl: Train journeys through the Western Ghats pass through many tunnels — a real-life mini adventure!

rv.summary: An adventure story has excitement, a challenge and a brave character. In our story Ishaan is scared of a dark train tunnel but stays calm by counting until bright fields appear. Stories have a setting, characters, problem, climax and resolution.
focus: Identify the setting, problem, climax and resolution of a story
Infer feelings from actions like gripping a bar
Explain how writers build suspense
remember: Climax = the most exciting or tense point; resolution = how the problem is solved
Suspense comes from short sentences, sound words and unanswered questions
Courage means facing your fear, not feeling no fear
traps: The climax is not the ending; the resolution is
'His heart drummed fast' means his heart beat quickly, not that he played a drum

topics.h: India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 — and today Indian Railways carries crores of people!
p: Railway words: platform, compartment (coach), engine (locomotive), track, signal, guard, tunnel.
Sound words (onomatopoeia) make a train come alive: chug-chug, whoosh, clang, rattle, toot.
India's first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 from Bori Bunder (Mumbai) to Thane.
Safety first: stand behind the yellow line on the platform and cross only by the footbridge.
A tunnel is a passage dug through a hill or under the ground.

ex.q: Which sound words could you use for a train leaving a station?
st: Think of the whistle → toot / whistle
Think of the engine starting → chug-chug
Think of wheels on the track → rattle / clatter
ex.a: toot, chug-chug, rattle — these are onomatopoeia

topics.rl: Next time you're at a railway station, listen for the announcements, the clang of the bell and the whistle of the engine.

rv.summary: Railway words include platform, compartment, engine, track, signal and tunnel, and sound words like chug-chug and toot make trains come alive. India's first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder to Thane on 16 April 1853.
focus: Know the meanings of common railway words
Use onomatopoeia for train sounds
Recall the first passenger train and platform safety rules
remember: Engine (locomotive) pulls the coaches; a compartment is a section where passengers sit
Onomatopoeia: chug-chug, whoosh, clang, rattle, toot
First passenger train: 16 April 1853, Bori Bunder (Mumbai) to Thane
Stand behind the yellow line; cross only by the footbridge
traps: The first train ran in 1853, not 1857
Don't cross the tracks to save time

topics.h: 'I was waiting when the train came.' — two past tenses in one sentence, working as a team!
p: Simple past tells about a finished action: The train arrived at six.
Past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) tells about an action in progress in the past: I was waiting.
Together: 'While we were waiting, the train arrived.' The longer action is past continuous; the short one that interrupts is simple past.
Use 'was' with I, he, she, it and singular nouns; 'were' with you, we, they and plural nouns.
Watch irregular verbs: run → ran, catch → caught, ring → rang; and spelling: stop → stopped.

ex.q: Fix this sentence: 'I was eat my lunch when the train come.'
st: The longer action is in progress → was + eating
The short action interrupts → simple past 'came'
ex.a: I was eating my lunch when the train came.

topics.rl: When you tell a friend what happened on a trip, you naturally use both tenses: 'We were singing when the bus stopped!'

rv.summary: The simple past tells about a finished action, and the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) tells about an action in progress. When used together, the longer action is past continuous and the short interrupting action is simple past.
focus: Form the past continuous with was/were + verb-ing
Combine past continuous and simple past with 'while' and 'when'
Learn irregular past forms and spelling rules
remember: was with I, he, she, it and singular nouns; were with you, we, they and plurals
'While we were waiting, the train arrived.'
run → ran, catch → caught, ring → rang; stop → stopped
traps: Don't write 'was eat'; it is 'was eating'
Children takes 'were', not 'was'
Don't add -ed to irregular verbs (runned, catched)

topics.t: A poem of longing to travel
topics.h: Have you ever heard a train at night and wondered where it was going?
p: 'Travel' is a poem in which the speaker hears trains and longs to go on a journey. Here is our own poem on that feeling.
Longing means a strong wish for something you do not have.
The speaker is the voice in the poem (the 'I'); it may or may not be the poet.
Mood is the feeling a poem creates — here it is dreamy and restless.
Poets use personification ('a whistle calls my name') and similes ('like flame') to show feelings.

ex.q: Read: Each night a far-off whistle calls my name, / The lights of passing trains go by like flame. / My books stay open, but my thoughts have flown / To mountain roads and towns I've never known. How does the speaker feel, and which words show it?
st: 'calls my name' — the speaker feels the journey is calling.
'my thoughts have flown' — the mind is already far away.
'towns I've never known' — a wish to see new places.
ex.a: The speaker feels a restless longing to travel; 'calls my name', 'thoughts have flown' and 'towns I've never known' show it.

topics.rl: Looking at a map, a travel show or an aeroplane in the sky and wishing you were going somewhere — that's longing!

rv.summary: In this poem the speaker hears a far-off train whistle and longs to travel, daydreaming instead of studying. The poem's mood is dreamy and restless, shown through personification and similes.
focus: Explain the speaker's longing and the poem's mood
Spot personification and similes in lines
Find rhyming words
remember: Longing = a strong wish for something you do not have
The speaker is the voice ('I') in the poem; it may not be the poet
'a far-off whistle calls my name' = personification; 'go by like flame' = simile
traps: 'Like flame' is a simile, not a metaphor
The speaker is not the reader
'My thoughts have flown' means daydreaming, not books flying

topics.h: Close your eyes: 'hot, crispy pakoras on a rainy evening'. Can you smell them? That's imagery!
p: Imagery is language that helps us see, hear, smell, taste or feel something in our minds.
Sight imagery: 'golden mustard fields'. Sound imagery: 'the engine roared'.
Smell imagery: 'the scent of wet earth'. Taste: 'tangy chaat'. Touch: 'the cold window glass'.
Strong imagery uses exact nouns, vivid adjectives and strong verbs.
Compare: 'The train went.' with 'The train thundered over the iron bridge.'

ex.q: Make this sentence vivid: 'The bus went up the hill.'
st: Add a colour or detail: red bus
Choose a strong verb: rattled
Add a setting detail: misty hill
ex.a: The red bus rattled up the misty hill.

topics.rl: Travel posters, food ads and good storybooks use imagery to make you want to go, taste or read more.

rv.summary: Imagery is language that helps us see, hear, smell, taste or feel something in our minds. Writers create strong imagery with exact nouns, vivid adjectives and strong verbs.
focus: Match a line of imagery to the sense it appeals to
Make plain sentences vivid
Choose strong verbs and adjectives
remember: Sight: golden mustard fields; sound: the engine roared
Smell: the scent of wet earth; taste: tangy chaat; touch: the cold window glass
'The train went.' → 'The train thundered over the iron bridge.'
traps: Colours are sight imagery, not touch
Weak verbs like 'went', 'was', 'did' create little imagery

topics.h: At the top of Mount Everest, the air has only about one-third as much oxygen as at sea level!
p: 'Conquering the Summit' is about mountaineering and the grit it takes to reach the top.
Mount Everest (8,849 m) is the highest mountain in the world. It lies on the border of Nepal and China (Tibet).
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary were the first to reach its summit, on 29 May 1953.
Bachendri Pal became the first Indian woman to climb Everest, in 1984.
Mountaineering words: summit, base camp, expedition, altitude, ice axe, crampons, oxygen cylinder.

ex.q: Why do climbers on very high mountains carry oxygen cylinders?
st: Altitude means height above sea level.
The higher you go, the thinner the air, so there is less oxygen in each breath.
Extra oxygen helps climbers breathe and stay safe.
ex.a: Because the air at great heights has much less oxygen, so they carry extra oxygen to breathe safely.

topics.rl: Mountaineering institutes in Darjeeling, Uttarkashi and Manali train young climbers in safety and teamwork.

rv.summary: Mountaineering takes grit. Mount Everest (8,849 m), on the Nepal–China border, was first climbed by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary in 1953, and Bachendri Pal was the first Indian woman to climb it, in 1984.
focus: Recall key facts about Mount Everest and its first climbers
Know mountaineering words like summit, base camp, expedition and altitude
Explain why climbers carry oxygen
remember: Mount Everest: 8,849 m, on the border of Nepal and China (Tibet)
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary: first to the summit, 29 May 1953
Bachendri Pal: first Indian woman on Everest, 1984
Summit = highest point; base camp = main camp at the foot of a mountain
traps: Everest is on the Nepal–China border, not India–Nepal
Bachendri Pal did not climb with Tenzing in 1953
Climbers carry oxygen because thin air has less of it

topics.h: Add '-ation' to 'determine' and you get the one word every mountaineer needs: determination!
p: Determination is a strong will to reach your goal, even when it is hard.
Suffixes are added at the end of a word and can change its class: determine → determination, achieve → achievement.
-ous, -ful and -less make adjectives: courage → courageous, hope → hopeful, fear → fearless. (-ful = full of; -less = without)
-ly makes many adverbs: brave → bravely, tireless → tirelessly.
A character's actions show their qualities: trying again every day shows determination.

ex.q: Read: When Pema first tried to climb the hill behind her school in Sikkim, she stopped halfway, out of breath. The next morning, she tried again. Every day she climbed a little higher, carrying her water bottle and a smile. By winter, she reached the top without stopping and saw the snowy peaks glowing in the sun. Which quality does Pema show, and which words prove it?
st: She stopped halfway at first.
'The next morning, she tried again.' and 'Every day she climbed a little higher.'
She did not give up until she reached the top.
ex.a: Determination — she tried again every day until she reached the top.

topics.rl: Athletes, students preparing for exams and farmers waiting for the monsoon all need determination.

rv.summary: Determination is a strong will to reach a goal even when it is hard. Suffixes build new words: -ation and -ment make nouns, -ous, -ful and -less make adjectives, and -ly makes adverbs.
focus: Add suffixes to form nouns, adjectives and adverbs
Know the meanings of -ful (full of) and -less (without)
Find a character's quality from their actions
remember: determine → determination; achieve → achievement
courage → courageous; hope → hopeful; fear → fearless
tireless → tirelessly (adverb)
-ful = full of; -less = without
traps: Hopeless means without hope, not full of hope
Use an adverb (tirelessly) to describe how someone works
Don't make up forms like courageful or achieveness

topics.h: 'She has climbed Everest!' — the present perfect connects a past action to right now.
p: Present perfect = has/have + past participle: She has climbed. They have reached.
Use 'has' with he, she, it and singular nouns; 'have' with I, you, we, they and plural nouns.
It is used for actions finished at an unstated time or with a result now; words like just, already, yet, ever, never go with it.
Do not use it with a definite past time (yesterday, in 1953) — use simple past: 'Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.'
'Since' + a point of time (since 2019); 'for' + a length of time (for six months).

ex.q: Choose correctly: 'Riya (has reached / reached) base camp yesterday.'
st: 'Yesterday' is a definite past time.
The present perfect is not used with a definite past time.
So we use simple past.
ex.a: Riya reached base camp yesterday.

topics.rl: News headlines often use the present perfect: 'Indian team has won the gold!'

rv.summary: The present perfect is has/have + past participle. It is used for actions finished at an unstated time or with a result now, often with just, already, yet, ever and never, but not with a definite past time.
focus: Form the present perfect with has or have
Choose between present perfect and simple past
Use since and for correctly
remember: has with he, she, it and singular nouns; have with I, you, we, they and plurals
go – went – gone; see – saw – seen
Definite past time (yesterday, in 1953) → simple past
since + point of time (since 2020); for + length of time (for three months)
traps: Don't say 'has reached in 1953'; say 'reached in 1953'
Don't use the simple past form after have: have seen, not have saw
Don't mix up since and for

topics.ch: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
topics.h: Whether it is snowy mountains, deep seas or the open sky, someone is keeping watch over India every minute.
p: 'A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers' honours the men and women who protect our country. Homage means deep respect shown to honour someone.
India's armed forces are the Army (land), the Navy (sea) and the Air Force (air).
The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.
Army Day is on 15 January, Air Force Day on 8 October and Navy Day on 4 December.
Soldiers also help people during floods, earthquakes and other disasters with rescue and relief.

ex.q: A flood hits a village. Which forces might help, and how?
st: The Army can rescue people and set up relief camps.
The Navy can send boats and divers.
The Air Force can fly helicopters to drop food and lift people to safety.
ex.a: All three can help: the Army on land, the Navy with boats and divers, and the Air Force with helicopters.

topics.rl: On Republic Day, the parade on Kartavya Path in New Delhi shows marching contingents of the Army, Navy and Air Force.

rv.summary: This lesson pays homage to the soldiers who protect India. Our armed forces are the Army, Navy and Air Force, with the President as Supreme Commander, and soldiers also help people during disasters.
focus: Match each force to land, sea or air
Recall Army Day, Air Force Day and Navy Day dates
Know the role of soldiers in disaster relief
remember: Army = land, Navy = sea, Air Force = air
The President of India is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces
Army Day 15 January; Air Force Day 8 October; Navy Day 4 December
Homage = deep respect shown to honour someone
traps: The Prime Minister is not the Supreme Commander
Don't mix up Army Day (15 January) with Republic Day (26 January)

topics.ch: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
topics.h: 'Param Vir' means 'the bravest of the brave' — the name of India's highest wartime gallantry award.
p: Patriotism means love for one's country; a patriot is a person who loves and serves the country.
Sacrifice means giving up something precious for the sake of others.
Gallantry and valour both mean great bravery. Valiant means very brave; its opposite is cowardly.
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime gallantry award; the Ashoka Chakra is the highest peacetime gallantry award.
The National War Memorial in New Delhi honours soldiers who gave their lives for the nation.

ex.q: Why do people stand in silence at a war memorial?
st: A memorial reminds us of soldiers who gave their lives.
Silence is a way of showing deep respect.
It helps us remember their sacrifice.
ex.a: To show respect and remember the soldiers' sacrifice for the nation.

topics.rl: Many schools collect money on Armed Forces Flag Day (7 December) for the welfare of soldiers and their families.

rv.summary: Patriotism is love for one's country, and sacrifice means giving up something precious for others. India honours bravery with awards like the Param Vir Chakra (wartime) and the Ashoka Chakra (peacetime), and the National War Memorial in New Delhi remembers fallen soldiers.
focus: Know the meanings of patriotism, sacrifice, valour, gallantry and valiant
Tell wartime and peacetime gallantry awards apart
Find synonyms and antonyms of brave
remember: Patriotism = love for one's country; sacrifice = giving up something precious for others
Valour and gallantry = great bravery; valiant = very brave; opposite: cowardly
Param Vir Chakra: highest wartime gallantry award; Ashoka Chakra: highest peacetime gallantry award
National War Memorial: New Delhi
traps: Bharat Ratna is a civilian award, not a gallantry award
Don't swap the Param Vir Chakra (war) and the Ashoka Chakra (peace)
Timid and nervous are not synonyms of brave

topics.ch: A Homage to Our Brave Soldiers
topics.h: 'The soldier saved the child' or 'The child was saved by the soldier' — same event, different focus!
p: In the active voice, the subject does the action: The soldiers built the bridge.
In the passive voice, the subject receives the action: The bridge was built by the soldiers.
Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle (+ by the doer).
Simple present passive: is/are + past participle. Simple past passive: was/were + past participle.
We use the passive when the doer is unknown or less important: The fort was built long ago.

ex.q: Change to passive: 'The Navy rescued the fishermen.'
st: Object 'the fishermen' becomes the subject.
Past tense, plural subject → were + past participle 'rescued'.
Add 'by the Navy'.
ex.a: The fishermen were rescued by the Navy.

topics.rl: News reports often use the passive: 'Hundreds of people were rescued from the floods.'

rv.summary: In the active voice the subject does the action; in the passive voice the subject receives it. The passive uses a form of 'be' + past participle (+ by the doer) and is used when the doer is unknown or less important.
focus: Change active sentences into passive and back
Choose is/are/was/were to match subject and tense
Use the correct past participle
remember: Active: The soldiers built the bridge. → Passive: The bridge was built by the soldiers.
Simple present passive: is/are + past participle; simple past passive: was/were + past participle
write – wrote – written; give – gave – given
traps: Don't use the simple past form in the passive (were wrote); use the past participle (were written)
Match the helping verb to the new subject: the villagers are helped
Don't swap the doer and the receiver when changing voice

topics.h: The Siachen Glacier is called the world's highest battlefield — soldiers guard it in freezing cold!
p: 'My Dear Soldiers' is a poem that thanks and honours our soldiers. Here is our own tribute poem.
A tribute is something said, written or done to show respect and thanks.
Poets use contrast to show how tough a soldier's job is: icy Siachen and the hot Thar Desert.
The Siachen Glacier in Ladakh is known as the highest battlefield in the world.
The tone of such poems is grateful, proud and respectful.

ex.q: Read: On Siachen's ice where the cold winds blow, / In Thar's hot sands where few dare go, / On stormy seas and skies so high, / You stand on guard as days roll by. / We sleep in peace, we laugh, we play — / Dear soldiers, thank you, every day. What contrast does the poet show, and what is the tone?
st: Cold 'Siachen's ice' is set against 'Thar's hot sands'.
Soldiers guard land, sea and sky.
'Dear soldiers, thank you' shows gratitude.
ex.a: The poet contrasts freezing ice with hot sand to show soldiers guard everywhere; the tone is grateful and respectful.

topics.rl: Students across India send rakhis, cards and letters to soldiers posted at the borders to say thank you.

rv.summary: This tribute poem thanks soldiers who guard India everywhere, from icy Siachen, the world's highest battlefield, to the hot Thar Desert. Its contrasts show how tough their work is, and its tone is grateful and respectful.
focus: Explain the contrasts in the poem and what they show
Identify the tone of a tribute poem
Find rhyming words and explain phrases like 'as days roll by'
remember: Tribute = something said, written or done to show respect and thanks
Siachen Glacier (Ladakh) = highest battlefield in the world; Thar = hot desert, mostly in Rajasthan
Tone: grateful, proud and respectful
traps: A tribute is not a limerick (funny poem)
Siachen is an icy glacier, not a desert

topics.h: 'Thank you' is two small words, but it can make someone's whole day brighter!
p: Gratitude means feeling thankful and showing it.
Words of thanks: grateful, thankful, appreciate, indebted.
Use 'grateful to' a person and 'grateful for' a thing: I am grateful to my teacher for her help.
A thank-you note has a greeting, what you are thankful for, how it helped you, and a warm closing.
Spelling tip: it is 'grateful', not 'greatful'.

ex.q: Write one line for a thank-you note to a soldier.
st: Say what you are thankful for: keeping our borders safe.
Say how it helps: we can study and play without fear.
Be specific and sincere.
ex.a: Thank you for keeping our borders safe; because of you, we can study and play without fear.

topics.rl: Thank-you cards on Teachers' Day, a 'thank you' to the bus driver, or a letter to a soldier — gratitude is everywhere.

rv.summary: Gratitude means feeling thankful and showing it. We are grateful to a person and grateful for a thing, and a good thank-you note says what we are thankful for and how it helped.
focus: Spell grateful correctly and know its opposite and noun
Use grateful to and grateful for correctly
Write a good line for a thank-you note
remember: Correct spelling: grateful (not greatful); noun: gratitude; opposite: ungrateful
grateful TO a person, grateful FOR a thing
Appreciate = to value something and be thankful for it
traps: Don't write 'greatful'
Don't say 'grateful for my teacher'; say 'grateful to my teacher'
'Thanks, bye' is too short for a good thank-you note

topics.t: The queen who fought the Portuguese
topics.h: Over 450 years ago, a queen of a small coastal kingdom in Karnataka refused to bow to a powerful European navy!
p: Rani Abbakka Chowta ruled Ullal, a port town near Mangaluru on the coast of present-day Karnataka, in the 16th century.
The Portuguese came to India by sea; Vasco da Gama reached Kozhikode (Calicut) in 1498, and the Portuguese captured Goa in 1510.
The Portuguese wanted to control the ports and the spice trade and demanded tribute (payment) from local rulers.
Rani Abbakka refused to pay and fought them for many years. She is remembered as 'Abhaya Rani' — the fearless queen.
She is honoured as one of the earliest Indian rulers to resist European powers.

ex.q: Why did the Portuguese want Ullal, and how did Rani Abbakka respond?
st: Ullal was a busy port on the coast.
The Portuguese wanted control of the ports and trade and asked for tribute.
Abbakka refused and fought back.
ex.a: They wanted control of its port and trade; Rani Abbakka refused to pay tribute and fought them bravely.

topics.rl: Coastal Karnataka still honours her with statues, folk songs and a yearly festival in Ullal.

rv.summary: Rani Abbakka Chowta ruled the port town of Ullal, near Mangaluru, in the 16th century. When the Portuguese demanded tribute to control the ports and spice trade, she refused and fought them for years, earning the name 'Abhaya Rani'.
focus: Recall where and when Rani Abbakka ruled
Explain why the Portuguese wanted Ullal and how she responded
Know key dates of the Portuguese arrival and the meaning of tribute
remember: Rani Abbakka ruled Ullal, near Mangaluru (Karnataka), in the 16th century
Vasco da Gama reached Kozhikode (Calicut) in 1498; the Portuguese captured Goa in 1510
Tribute (in history) = payment forced by a stronger power
Abhaya Rani = the fearless queen
traps: She fought the Portuguese, not the British
Ullal is in Karnataka, not Goa or Kerala
In history, tribute means a forced payment, not a poem of praise

topics.h: A true leader is not the loudest person in the room — it's the one people trust to find a way.
p: A leader guides a group, makes decisions and takes responsibility.
Good leaders show courage, honesty, fairness, calmness and teamwork, and they listen to others.
Courage can be quiet too — like standing up for what is right.
A character's actions reveal their qualities: we don't need to be told someone is a leader if we see them lead.
Word family: lead (verb), leader (person), leadership (quality).

ex.q: Read: When the school fair got rained out, class monitor Leela did not panic. She split the class into teams: one moved the stalls under the verandah, one dried the chairs, and one made new signboards. By noon, the fair was buzzing again. "A leader listens and then acts," her teacher smiled. Which leadership qualities does Leela show?
st: 'did not panic' → calm
'split the class into teams' → plans and shares work
The fair was saved → she takes responsibility.
ex.a: Leela is calm, plans well, shares work fairly and takes responsibility.

topics.rl: Class monitors, sports captains and team leaders in school projects all practise leadership every day.

rv.summary: A leader guides a group, makes decisions and takes responsibility. Good leaders are calm, fair and brave, listen before acting and share work, as Leela does when rain spoils the school fair.
focus: Find leadership qualities from a character's actions
Know the word family lead, leader, leadership
Find synonyms and antonyms of courageous and leader
remember: lead (verb), leader (person), leadership (quality)
Good leaders show courage, honesty, fairness, calmness and teamwork
Responsibility = a duty you are trusted to do
Courageous = bold; opposite of leader = follower
traps: Leadership is not taking all the credit or blaming others
'Leader' is the person; 'leadership' is the quality

topics.h: 'And', 'but', 'so', 'because' — joining words are the glue of good sentences!
p: Conjunctions are joining words that join words, phrases or sentences.
'And' adds; 'but' shows contrast; 'or' gives a choice; 'so' shows a result; 'because' gives a reason.
'Although' (or 'though') shows contrast inside one sentence: Although the enemy was strong, the queen did not give up.
Don't use 'but' with 'although' in the same sentence.
'Until' means up to the time when: Wait here until I come back.

ex.q: Join with the right conjunction: 'The Portuguese had big ships. Abbakka did not give up.'
st: The second idea is a surprise after the first → contrast.
Contrast conjunctions: but / although.
ex.a: The Portuguese had big ships, but Abbakka did not give up. (Or: Although the Portuguese had big ships, Abbakka did not give up.)

topics.rl: Whenever you explain why you are late or what you did on the weekend, you use 'because', 'so' and 'and' without thinking!

rv.summary: Conjunctions join words, phrases or sentences. And adds, but shows contrast, or gives a choice, so shows a result, because gives a reason, although shows contrast within one sentence and until means up to the time when.
focus: Choose the right conjunction for addition, contrast, choice, result or reason
Join two sentences using although
Avoid using 'but' together with 'although'
remember: and = adds; but = contrast; or = choice; so = result; because = reason
Although it rained, we played. (no 'but')
until = up to the time when
traps: Don't write 'Although…, but…'
Don't confuse 'so' (result) with 'because' (reason)

qa.q: 'Every morning, Meera sat on the steps by the river and watched children walk to school.' What is the setting of this line?
qa.a: The steps by a river, in the morning
qa.e: The line says Meera sat 'on the steps by the river' 'every morning' — that is the place and time.

qa.q: '"I want to read books too," Meera whispered.' What does Meera wish for?
qa.a: To study and read like the other children
qa.e: She says she wants to read books 'too', like the children going to school.

qa.q: 'The river splashed softly and said, "Go on, little one."' Which figure of speech is used here?
qa.e: A river cannot speak, so giving it speech is personification.

qa.q: Which sentence uses personification?
qa.a: The river sang a soft song to the girl.
qa.e: Only a person can sing a song; giving this action to a river is personification.

qa.q: 'Meera whispered her wish so that no one could hear.' This most likely shows that she feels:
qa.e: Whispering so no one hears suggests she is shy or not sure anyone will listen.

qa.q: What is the theme of a story?
qa.a: The big idea or message the story shares
qa.e: The theme is the central idea, like 'every child deserves to learn'.

qa.q: '"Even I keep moving forward," said the river.' What lesson does the river give Meera?
qa.a: Keep going and don't stop trying
qa.e: A river always flows on; it tells Meera to keep moving towards her goal.

qa.q: 'The next day, Meera asked her father if she could join the village school.' This shows that Meera:
qa.a: found the courage to act on her wish
qa.e: She moves from only wishing to actually asking — that takes courage.

qa.q: Which word means 'able to read and write'?
qa.e: Literate means able to read and write. Literature means books and writing; literal means exact.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'literate'?
qa.e: The prefix il- is used before words starting with l: literate → illiterate.

qa.q: India's Right to Education Act gives free and compulsory schooling to children aged:
qa.e: The Right to Education Act, 2009 covers children from 6 to 14 years of age.

qa.q: Who, along with Jyotirao Phule, started a school for girls in Pune in 1848?
qa.e: Savitribai Phule taught at the girls' school she and Jyotirao Phule started in Pune in 1848.

qa.q: Which word in this family is a noun: educate, education, educated, educational?
qa.e: 'Education' names a thing (the process of learning). 'Educate' is a verb; 'educated' and 'educational' are adjectives.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'My aunt is an ___ woman; she has a college degree.'
qa.e: An adjective is needed to describe 'woman', so 'educated' fits.

qa.q: 'Ritu teaches her grandmother to read the names on bus boards.' What does this tell us?
qa.a: People can learn at any age
qa.e: Nani is learning to read in her old age, so learning has no age limit.

qa.q: Which sentence BEST matches the idea of 'education for all'?
qa.a: Every child, girl or boy, should get the chance to learn.
qa.e: 'For all' means everyone — every girl and every boy, in villages and cities.

qa.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
qa.e: Kaveri is the special name of one river, so it is a proper noun and starts with a capital letter.

qa.q: Which of these is an abstract noun?
qa.e: Honesty is a quality — you cannot see or touch it. The others are things or people.

qa.q: 'A herd of elephants crossed the river.' Which word is the collective noun?
qa.e: 'Herd' is the name for a group of elephants.

qa.q: Complete: 'a ___ of fish'
qa.e: A group of fish swimming together is called a school (or shoal).

qa.q: Which words need capital letters in: 'meera visited jaipur in december.'?
qa.e: The first word of a sentence and proper nouns (a name, a city, a month) begin with capital letters.

qa.q: 'Her kindness made everyone smile.' The word 'kindness' is:
qa.e: Kindness is a quality we feel but cannot touch, so it is an abstract noun.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'brave'?
qa.e: 'Bravery' names the quality. 'Bravely' is an adverb; 'braver' and 'bravest' are adjectives.

qa.q: Complete: 'a ___ of wolves'
qa.e: A group of wolves is called a pack.

qa.q: 'My kite fell down, it tore in two, / I sighed, "Now what am I to do?"' Which word rhymes with 'two'?
qa.e: 'Two' and 'do' end with the same 'oo' sound.

qa.q: The lines of a poem end with: two, do, tail, fail. What is the rhyme scheme?
qa.e: two/do rhyme (a a), tail/fail rhyme (b b), so the scheme is aabb.

qa.q: What does 'perseverance' mean?
qa.a: continuing to try in spite of difficulty
qa.e: Perseverance is not stopping when things are hard.

qa.q: 'I tied the string, I fixed the tail, / I tried again — this time, no fail!' What did the child do after the kite tore?
qa.e: The child tied the string, fixed the tail and tried again.

qa.q: 'If once you slip, then rise and say...' In this poem, 'slip' most nearly means:
qa.e: Here 'slip' is used to mean failing once, and 'rise' means trying again.

qa.q: A group of lines in a poem is called a:
qa.e: Poems are divided into stanzas; stories into paragraphs and chapters; plays into scenes.

qa.q: A line or phrase that is repeated again and again in a poem is called a:
qa.e: A refrain is a repeated line, like 'try again' in many poems on perseverance.

qa.q: Which proverb matches the message of the poem?
qa.a: If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
qa.e: The poem is about not giving up after failing — exactly what this proverb says.

qa.q: 'Don't give up!' means:
qa.e: The phrasal verb 'give up' means to stop trying or quit.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'determined'?
qa.e: Resolute means firm in purpose — the same as determined.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'patient'?
qa.e: Words starting with p often take im-: impatient, impossible, impolite.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'regular'?
qa.e: Before r, the prefix becomes ir-: irregular, irresponsible.

qa.q: 'Even after losing twice, Arjun did not quit. He decided to ___ practising.'
qa.e: He did not quit, so he decided to continue — 'carry on'.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'success'?
qa.e: Success means achieving your aim; failure means not achieving it.

qa.q: Which word means 'continuing firmly and not stopping trying'?
qa.e: A persistent person keeps on trying.

qa.q: What does 'Practice makes perfect' mean?
qa.a: Doing something again and again makes you better at it.
qa.e: Repeating and practising a skill is how we improve.

qa.q: How did Helen Keller lose her sight and hearing?
qa.a: After an illness when she was about 19 months old
qa.e: She became deaf and blind after an illness as a baby, at about 19 months.

qa.q: Who taught Helen Keller by spelling words into her hand?
qa.e: Anne Sullivan became Helen's teacher in 1887 and spelled words into her palm.

qa.q: 'Three Days to See' by Helen Keller is:
qa.e: It is written in prose and shares the writer's thoughts — an essay.

qa.q: What is an essay?
qa.a: A short piece of prose on one subject, giving the writer's ideas
