qa.e: Essays are in prose (not verse) and share a writer's thoughts on one topic.

qa.q: What is the main message of 'Three Days to See'?
qa.a: We should use our senses fully and not take them for granted
qa.e: Helen Keller urges sighted people to look closely at the world as if they might lose their sight tomorrow.

qa.q: Helen Keller was the first deafblind person to earn:
qa.e: She graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904 with a BA degree.

qa.q: 'If I could see for just one day, I would first look at my mother's face.' What would the writer look at first?
qa.e: The word 'first' tells us the mother's face comes before the garland and the stars.

qa.q: To 'take something for granted' means to:
qa.a: not value it because you always have it
qa.e: When we take sight for granted, we forget how precious it is.

qa.q: Which word appeals to our sense of hearing?
qa.e: Rustling is the sound of dry leaves or paper moving.

qa.q: 'The mogra flowers were fragrant.' Which sense does 'fragrant' appeal to?
qa.e: Fragrant means having a sweet smell.

qa.q: Who invented the Braille system of reading?
qa.e: Louis Braille of France created the raised-dot system that is named after him.

qa.q: How many dot positions are there in one Braille cell?
qa.e: A Braille cell has 6 dot positions in two columns of three; different patterns stand for different letters.

qa.q: Which word appeals to our sense of touch?
qa.e: Rough describes how something feels to our skin.

qa.q: Which sense organ helps us taste food?
qa.e: Taste buds on the tongue tell sweet, sour, salty and bitter.

qa.q: What does 'melodious' mean?
qa.e: Melodious comes from 'melody' — a tune — so it means pleasant to hear.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the sense of taste?
qa.e: Sour is a taste.

qa.q: What is the comparative degree of 'good'?
qa.e: 'Good' is irregular: good – better – best.

qa.q: What is the superlative degree of 'bad'?
qa.e: 'Bad' is irregular: bad – worse – worst.

qa.q: Which sentence is correct?
qa.a: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
qa.e: Comparing with all mountains needs the superlative with 'the': the highest.

qa.q: What is the comparative degree of 'happy'?
qa.e: When an adjective ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happier.

qa.q: 'Of all my senses, I think sight is the ___ precious.'
qa.e: 'Of all' compares many, so we need the superlative 'most'.

qa.q: What is the comparative degree of 'big'?
qa.e: Short words ending in one vowel + one consonant double the last letter: big → bigger.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the positive degree?
qa.e: 'Tall' describes Ravi without comparing — positive degree.

qa.q: 'In May, Delhi is ___ than Shimla.'
qa.e: Two places are compared with 'than', so the comparative 'hotter' is needed.

qa.q: Who created the character Doctor Dolittle?
qa.e: Hugh Lofting, an English writer, wrote the Doctor Dolittle books.

qa.q: In the Doctor Dolittle stories, who teaches the doctor the language of animals?
qa.e: His parrot Polynesia teaches him to understand animals. Jip and Chee-Chee are other animal friends.

qa.q: A doctor who treats animals is called a:
qa.e: Veterinarians (vets) treat animals. A paediatrician treats children; an optician deals with eyes and glasses.

qa.q: 'A goat with a sore hoof bleated, "Ma-a-a!"' The sound a goat makes is called a:
qa.e: Goats and sheep bleat. Horses neigh, elephants trumpet and owls hoot.

qa.q: 'Mynah flapped her wings and explained the problem to the doctor. "What would I do without my translator?" said Dr Mehta.' Why is Mynah called a translator?
qa.a: She changes the animals' words into words the doctor understands
qa.e: A translator changes one language into another; Mynah turns animal talk into human words.

qa.q: What does 'translate' mean?
qa.a: to change words from one language into another
qa.e: To translate is to put words into a different language.

qa.q: Which of these is a REAL way animals communicate?
qa.a: Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
qa.e: The honeybee's waggle dance is a real way of sharing information. The others are fantasy.

qa.q: 'Dr Mehta's clinic was full of patients — but none of them were people!' Why is this line funny?
qa.a: We expect patients to be humans, but they are animals
qa.e: The surprise twist — the patients are animals — makes us smile.

qa.q: Which sentence is fantasy?
qa.a: A tiger opens a sweet shop in Kolkata.
qa.e: Tigers cannot run shops, so that sentence is fantasy.

qa.q: Which sentence is realistic?
qa.a: A dog barks at the postman.
qa.e: Dogs really do bark at strangers; the others cannot happen.

qa.q: 'This bag weighs a ton!' is an example of:
qa.e: A school bag doesn't really weigh a ton; the speaker is exaggerating for effect.

qa.q: Why do writers add humour to stories?
qa.a: To entertain readers and make them smile
qa.e: Humour makes reading fun and keeps us interested.

qa.q: What does 'imaginary' mean?
qa.e: Something imaginary is made up, not real.

qa.q: Which word in this family is a noun: imagine, imagination, imaginary, imaginative?
qa.e: 'Imagination' names the ability; 'imagine' is a verb and the other two are adjectives.

qa.q: Which sentence uses exaggeration?
qa.a: I'm so hungry I could eat a whole elephant!
qa.e: Nobody can eat an elephant — the speaker exaggerates to show great hunger.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'serious'?
qa.e: Grave, solemn and stern all mean serious; funny is the opposite.

qa.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
qa.e: A comma after 'said', quotation marks around the exact words, a capital T, and the full stop inside the closing marks.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: Arun said, "I am hungry."
qa.a: Arun said that he was hungry.
qa.e: 'I' becomes 'he' and 'am' moves back to 'was'.

qa.q: In reported speech after 'said', 'will' usually changes to:
qa.e: The past form of 'will' is 'would'.

qa.q: Which sentence is in direct speech?
qa.e: Direct speech shows the exact words inside quotation marks.

qa.q: What do quotation marks show?
qa.e: Quotation marks (inverted commas) go around a speaker's exact words.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: Sita said, "I can swim."
qa.a: Sita said that she could swim.
qa.e: 'I' becomes 'she', and 'can' becomes 'could' followed by the base verb 'swim'.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: The teacher said, "The Earth goes around the Sun."
qa.a: The teacher said that the Earth goes around the Sun.
qa.e: A universal truth stays in the simple present even in reported speech.

qa.q: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk" — where should the question mark go?
qa.e: The question mark belongs to the spoken question, so it goes inside: Ravi asked, "Can animals talk?"

qa.q: 'Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands.' Why is this line funny?
qa.a: Shoes belong on feet, so it is a silly, upside-down action
qa.e: Wearing shoes on hands is the opposite of what we expect — that surprise is funny.

qa.q: 'Uncle Bholu wore his shoes on his hands, / And sang to the goats in the sugarcane lands.' Which word rhymes with 'hands'?
qa.e: 'Hands' and 'lands' end with the same '-ands' sound.

qa.q: Two lines next to each other that rhyme are called a:
qa.e: A couplet is a pair of rhyming lines.

qa.q: 'He laughed till his glasses went click-clack!' The words 'click-clack' are an example of:
qa.e: 'Click-clack' imitates the sound itself — that is onomatopoeia.

qa.q: What is rhythm in a poem?
qa.a: the beat or pattern of sounds
qa.e: Rhythm is the beat you feel when you read a poem aloud.

qa.q: The four lines of a poem end with: sun, bed, fun, red. What is the rhyme scheme?
qa.e: sun/fun rhyme (a), bed/red rhyme (b), and they alternate: a b a b.

qa.q: A 'humorous' poem is one that is:
qa.e: Humorous comes from 'humour', which means fun and laughter.

qa.q: 'He rode on a bullock cart, facing the back.' What does 'facing the back' mean?
qa.a: looking towards the rear instead of the front
qa.e: He sat turned around, looking where the cart had been — which is funny.

qa.q: Which pair are homophones?
qa.e: Flour and flower sound the same but are spelt differently and mean different things.

qa.q: 'Mr Mehta made many mango milkshakes.' This sentence shows:
qa.e: Many words start with the same 'm' sound — that is alliteration.

qa.q: Which word is a palindrome?
qa.e: L-E-V-E-L reads the same from both ends.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'We bought a kilo of ___ to make rotis.'
qa.e: Flour is the powder made from grain; a flower grows on a plant.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'The knight rode through the dark ___.'
qa.e: 'Night' means the dark time; 'knight' is a soldier on horseback.

qa.q: 'Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tired!' The word 'two-tired' sounds like:
qa.e: The pun works because 'two-tired' (two tyres) sounds like 'too tired'.

qa.q: Which Indian language's name is a palindrome?
qa.e: M-A-L-A-Y-A-L-A-M reads the same backwards.

qa.q: Which word is a homophone of 'week'?
qa.e: Week (seven days) and weak (not strong) sound the same.

qa.q: In a play, words in brackets like '(raising an eyebrow)' are called:
qa.e: They tell the actor what to do — they are stage directions.

qa.q: Do actors speak the stage directions aloud?
qa.a: No, stage directions only guide the actors
qa.e: Stage directions are instructions for actions and tone; they are not spoken.

qa.q: 'TINU: Amma, give me water!' 'AMMA: Is that how we ask?' Why does Amma say this?
qa.e: 'Give me water!' sounds like an order; Amma reminds him to ask nicely.

qa.q: The conversation between characters in a play is called:
qa.e: Dialogue is the talk between characters.

qa.q: The list of all the characters in a play is called the:
qa.e: The cast lists the characters (and sometimes the actors who play them).

qa.q: Plays are usually divided into:
qa.e: Acts are the big sections of a play; scenes are smaller parts inside them.

qa.q: 'TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water?' Which polite words does Tinu use?
qa.e: He asks with 'may I' and adds 'please' — a polite request.

qa.q: The people who watch a play are called the:
qa.e: The audience watches; the cast acts; the director guides the actors.

qa.q: What is the most polite way to ask for the salt at dinner?
qa.a: Could you please pass the salt?
qa.e: 'Could you please…' is a gentle, polite request.

qa.q: If you bump into someone by mistake, you should say:
qa.e: We say sorry when we have hurt or troubled someone, even by mistake.

qa.q: How should you ask to enter the staff room?
qa.e: 'May I…?' asks for permission politely.

qa.q: When someone says 'Thank you' to you, the best reply is:
qa.e: 'You're welcome' is the polite answer to thanks.

qa.q: Which phrase do we use to get someone's attention politely?
qa.e: 'Excuse me' is polite; the others can sound rude.

qa.q: In 'May I go out, sir?', the word 'may' shows:
qa.e: Here 'may' is used to ask permission.

qa.q: In 'Rani can swim very well', the word 'can' shows:
qa.e: 'Can' here tells us what Rani is able to do.

qa.q: Which sentence is a polite request?
qa.a: Would you help me carry these books, please?
qa.e: 'Would you… please?' turns an order into a polite request.

qa.q: What does 'a piece of cake' mean?
qa.e: 'The quiz was a piece of cake' means it was very easy.

qa.q: What does 'break the ice' mean?
qa.a: start a friendly conversation when people feel shy
qa.e: People 'break the ice' at a new class or party by talking first.

qa.q: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
qa.e: Something that happens once in a blue moon happens hardly ever.

qa.q: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
qa.e: It means to reveal a secret, often by accident.

qa.q: What does 'hold your horses' mean?
qa.e: It asks someone to slow down and wait.

qa.q: What does 'under the weather' mean?
qa.e: 'I'm under the weather' means 'I'm not feeling well.'

qa.q: Teacher: 'Use your head!' Golu taps his head on the desk. Why is this funny?
qa.a: Golu took the idiom literally; it means 'think carefully'
qa.e: 'Use your head' means think. Golu's literal action creates a funny misunderstanding.

qa.q: What does 'over the moon' mean?
qa.e: If you are over the moon, you are delighted.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'Kunal ___ a new machine from old spoons and a motor.'
qa.e: He made something new that did not exist before, so he invented it.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'Scientists have ___ a new kind of frog in the Western Ghats.'
qa.e: The frog already existed in nature; scientists found it, so they discovered it.

qa.q: A person who invents things is called an:
qa.e: Inventor is the person; invention is the thing made; inventive is an adjective.

qa.q: What does 'inventive' mean?
qa.a: creative and good at thinking of new ideas
qa.e: An inventive person comes up with new, clever ideas.

qa.q: '"Behold the Mango-Picker 3000!" he announced.' Here 'announced' means:
qa.a: said loudly and proudly to everyone
qa.e: To announce is to tell people something publicly, often with pride.

qa.q: 'The machine wobbled, buzzed and shook the branch — and one ripe mango dropped straight onto his head.' What happened?
qa.a: A mango fell on Kunal's head
qa.e: The machine shook the branch, and the mango dropped onto his head.

qa.q: 'Kunal rubbed his head and grinned. "Version two will have a basket."' This shows Kunal is:
qa.e: He smiles and plans a better version — he learns from the failure.

qa.q: Which day in India celebrates C. V. Raman's discovery of the Raman effect?
qa.e: National Science Day is celebrated on 28 February, the day Raman announced his discovery in 1928.

qa.q: One brother owns the robot. Which is correct?
qa.e: For one owner, add 's to the noun: brother's.

qa.q: Three sisters share a room. Which is correct?
qa.e: 'Sisters' is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe: sisters'.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'the ___ playground'
qa.e: 'Children' is already plural and doesn't end in s, so we add 's.

qa.q: What does 'siblings' mean?
qa.e: Siblings are children of the same parents.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'The cat licked ___ paw.'
qa.e: 'Its' shows belonging. 'It's' means 'it is', which doesn't fit here.

qa.q: Choose the right word: '___ raining, so take an umbrella.'
qa.e: We mean 'It is raining', so the short form is 'It's'.

qa.q: What does 'sibling rivalry' mean?
qa.e: Rivalry means competition; sibling rivalry is when brothers and sisters compete.

qa.q: Your father's sister is your:
qa.e: Your parent's sister is your aunt.

qa.q: Which is an imperative sentence?
qa.e: It gives a command and begins with the verb 'fold'.

qa.q: In 'Stir the mixture well', who is the understood subject?
qa.e: Imperative sentences speak to the listener, so 'you' is understood.

qa.q: Which word best begins the last step of instructions?
qa.e: 'Finally' signals the last step.

qa.q: 'Please shut the door.' What kind of sentence is this?
qa.e: It is a polite request or command, so it is imperative.

qa.q: 'What a clever invention!' What kind of sentence is this?
qa.e: It shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.

qa.q: 'Did your brother build this?' What kind of sentence is this?
qa.e: It asks a question and ends with a question mark.

qa.q: In written instructions, what usually comes before the steps?
qa.e: We first list what is needed, then give the steps.

qa.q: Choose the word to begin this step: '___ the seeds in wet cotton and keep them in a warm place.'
qa.e: Imperative steps begin with the base form of the verb: 'Put'.

qa.q: Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in:
qa.e: He won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature.

qa.q: In which year did Tagore win the Nobel Prize?
qa.e: Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

qa.q: Who wrote India's national anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana'?
qa.e: Tagore wrote it. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram', the national song.

qa.q: Santiniketan, where Tagore started his school, is in:
qa.e: Santiniketan is in West Bengal; the school grew into Visva-Bharati University.

qa.q: 'I draw a smiling sun in crayon blue — / Dear stranger, will this boat sail all the way to you?' Who does the child hope will find the boat?
qa.a: Someone far away whom the child has never met
qa.e: 'Dear stranger' and 'all the way to you' show the child hopes someone far away, whom the child does not know, will find the boat.

qa.q: 'Dear stranger, will this boat sail all the way to you?' A 'stranger' is:
qa.e: A stranger is a person you have never met.

qa.q: 'I fold my homework sheet into a boat, / And set it on the stream where raindrops float.' Which word rhymes with 'boat'?
qa.e: 'Boat' and 'float' both end with the '-oat' sound.

qa.q: What is the main feeling in the poem about the paper boat?
qa.e: The child dreams the boat will reach a faraway friend — a hopeful, wondering feeling.

qa.q: 'The paper boat floated like a leaf.' This is a:
qa.e: It compares the boat to a leaf using 'like'.

qa.q: 'The stream was a silver ribbon.' This is a:
qa.e: It says the stream IS a ribbon, without 'like' or 'as'.

qa.q: Complete the simile: 'as cool as a ___'
qa.e: 'As cool as a cucumber' means very calm.

qa.q: Complete the simile: 'as white as ___'
qa.e: Snow is very white, so 'as white as snow'.

qa.q: Which sentence is a metaphor?
qa.a: Dreams are wings that carry us far.
qa.e: It says dreams ARE wings — a metaphor. The others use 'like' or 'as'.

qa.q: Which word signals that a comparison is a simile?
qa.e: Similes use 'like' or 'as' to compare.

qa.q: 'Arjun dreams of becoming a pilot. One day he ___ fly planes.'
qa.e: 'One day' points to the future, so we use 'will'.

qa.q: Why do poets use similes and metaphors?
qa.a: To help readers picture things in a fresh way
qa.e: Comparisons create vivid pictures in the reader's mind.

qa.q: In a letter, 'Dear Anu,' is the:
qa.e: The salutation is the greeting that begins the letter.

qa.q: Which closing suits an informal letter to a friend?
qa.e: 'With love' is warm and suits family and friends.

qa.q: In a letter, the main part that carries your news is called the:
qa.e: The body is where you share your news and feelings.

qa.q: A letter to your school principal asking for leave is a:
qa.e: Letters to officials such as a principal are formal.

qa.q: 'Dear Anu, Greetings from Shillong! It rained three times today.' Where is Tara writing from?
qa.e: She says 'Greetings from Shillong!'

qa.q: 'The hills wore a cap of clouds.' What does this tell us?
qa.a: Clouds were resting on the tops of the hills
qa.e: A cap sits on top of a head, so the clouds were sitting on the hilltops.

qa.q: Where is the date usually written in a letter?
qa.a: near the top, below the sender's address
qa.e: The date comes at the top, just below the sender's address.

qa.q: What does 'P.S.' at the end of a letter mean?
qa.a: a note added after the letter is finished
qa.e: P.S. stands for postscript — something added after signing off.

qa.q: The sun rises in the:
qa.e: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

qa.q: Kanyakumari is at India's:
qa.e: Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu is the southernmost point of mainland India.

qa.q: Bihu is a festival and dance of:
qa.e: Bihu is celebrated in Assam.

qa.q: The Thar Desert lies mostly in:
qa.e: Most of the Thar Desert is in western Rajasthan.

qa.q: Kathakali is a classical dance from:
qa.e: Kathakali, with its colourful make-up, comes from Kerala.

qa.q: Which of these states is in the far west of India?
qa.e: Gujarat is on India's western coast. The others are in the North-east.

qa.q: Which direction is exactly opposite to north-east?
qa.e: Opposite of north is south and opposite of east is west, so north-east ↔ south-west.

qa.q: What does 'culture' mean?
qa.a: the way of life of a group — food, language, festivals and arts
qa.e: Culture is how people live, celebrate and express themselves.

qa.q: 'The boat sailed ___ the river to the other bank.'
qa.e: Across means from one side to the other.

qa.q: 'The cat ran ___ the house when it started raining.'
qa.e: 'Into' shows movement from outside to inside.

qa.q: 'The ball is ___ the table and the chair.'
qa.e: Two things are named, so we use 'between'.

qa.q: 'Share the sweets ___ all your classmates.'
qa.e: There are many classmates (more than two), so 'among' is correct.

qa.q: 'We waited ___ the bus stop for half an hour.'
qa.e: 'At' is used for a particular point or place like a bus stop.

qa.q: 'My cousin lives ___ Kolkata.'
qa.e: We use 'in' for cities and countries.

qa.q: 'The train went ___ a long tunnel.'
qa.e: 'Through' means in at one end and out at the other.

qa.q: 'Walk ___ the river bank to reach the temple.'
qa.e: 'Along' means moving beside the length of something.

qa.q: 'The moment the train entered the tunnel, the whole compartment went black.' What is the setting?
qa.a: A train passing through a tunnel
qa.e: The story takes place inside a train compartment in a tunnel.

qa.q: 'Ishaan gripped the window bar.' This shows that he felt:
qa.e: Gripping something tightly is a sign of nervousness.

qa.q: 'The wheels roared, and his heart drummed fast.' What does 'his heart drummed fast' mean?
qa.e: Like fast drumbeats, his heart was beating quickly with fear and excitement.

qa.q: 'He counted slowly — one, two, three…' Why did Ishaan count?
qa.a: To calm himself in the dark
qa.e: Counting slowly helps you stay calm when you are afraid.

qa.q: 'A burst of green and gold light flooded in: paddy fields and a sparkling river.' What did Ishaan see?
qa.e: The text names paddy fields and a sparkling river.

qa.q: The most exciting or tense point of a story is called the:
qa.e: The climax is the turning point, where tension is highest.

qa.q: The part of a story where the problem is solved is called the:
qa.e: The resolution comes at the end and ties things up.

qa.q: What does 'courage' best mean?
qa.a: facing your fear and doing what is needed
qa.e: Brave people may still feel fear, but they face it.

qa.q: Where do passengers wait for a train?
qa.e: The platform is the raised area beside the track where people wait.

qa.q: The part of a train that pulls the coaches is the:
qa.e: The engine (locomotive) pulls the coaches.

qa.q: 'The train's whistle went toot-toot.' The word 'toot-toot' is an example of:
qa.e: 'Toot-toot' imitates the sound of a whistle.

qa.q: India's first passenger train ran between:
qa.e: On 16 April 1853 the first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder to Thane.

qa.q: In which year did India's first passenger train run?
qa.e: It ran on 16 April 1853.

qa.q: What is the safe thing to do on a railway platform?
qa.e: Staying behind the yellow line keeps you away from moving trains.

qa.q: What is a 'compartment' in a train?
qa.a: one of the sections of a train where passengers sit
qa.e: A train has many compartments (coaches) for passengers.

qa.q: Which word is a sound word for a moving train?
qa.e: 'Chug' imitates the sound of an engine.

qa.q: 'While we ___ on the platform, the train came.'
qa.e: 'We' takes 'were', and the waiting was in progress: were waiting.

qa.q: 'Ishaan ___ out of the window when the lights went off.'
qa.e: The looking was in progress when the lights went off, so we use past continuous with 'was'.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'run'?
qa.e: 'Run' is irregular: run → ran.

qa.q: 'The children ___ when the whistle blew.'
qa.e: 'Children' is plural, so we use 'were playing'.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the past continuous tense?
qa.e: Was + reading (verb-ing) is past continuous.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'stop'?
qa.e: Short verbs ending in vowel + consonant double the consonant: stop → stopped.

qa.q: 'I was sleeping when the phone ___.'
qa.e: The short interrupting action is simple past: ring → rang.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'catch'?
qa.e: 'Catch' is irregular: catch → caught.

qa.q: What does 'longing' mean?
qa.e: Longing is a deep wish, such as a wish to travel.

qa.q: 'Each night a far-off whistle calls my name.' This line uses:
qa.e: A whistle cannot call a name; it is given a human action.

qa.q: 'The lights of passing trains go by like flame.' This line uses:
qa.e: The word 'like' compares the lights to flames.

qa.q: 'My books stay open, but my thoughts have flown.' What does this mean?
qa.a: The speaker is daydreaming about faraway places instead of studying
qa.e: The books are open, but the mind has wandered off to travel.

qa.q: What is the mood of the poem about the far-off whistle?
qa.e: The speaker is dreaming of roads and towns and cannot settle down to study.

qa.q: Who is the 'speaker' of a poem?
qa.a: the voice that tells the poem
qa.e: The speaker is the 'I' in the poem.

qa.q: '...my thoughts have flown / To mountain roads and towns I've never known.' Which word rhymes with 'known'?
qa.e: 'Flown' and 'known' end with the same '-own' (oh-n) sound.

qa.q: 'Each night a far-off whistle calls my name.' Which words show distance?
qa.e: 'Far-off' means far away.

qa.q: 'The engine roared and the whistle shrieked.' This line appeals mostly to our sense of:
qa.e: Roared and shrieked are sounds.

qa.q: 'The smell of hot pakoras drifted from the station stall.' Which sense does this appeal to?
qa.e: The line is about a smell.

qa.q: 'Golden mustard fields stretched to the sky.' Which sense does this appeal to?
qa.e: Colour and the wide view are things we see.

qa.q: 'The cold window glass pressed against my cheek.' Which sense does this appeal to?
qa.e: Feeling cold glass on your cheek is touch.

qa.q: 'The tangy chaat made my tongue tingle.' Which sense does this appeal to?
qa.e: Tangy food on the tongue is about taste.

qa.q: Which sentence has the strongest imagery?
qa.a: The red bus rattled up the misty hill.
qa.e: It gives colour, sound and setting — we can picture and hear it.

qa.q: What is imagery?
qa.a: language that appeals to our senses
qa.e: Imagery uses words to create pictures, sounds and feelings in the mind.

qa.q: Choose the strongest verb to replace 'went': 'The river ___ over the rocks.'
qa.e: 'Tumbled' shows how the water moved and helps us picture it.

qa.q: What does 'summit' mean?
qa.a: the highest point of a mountain
qa.e: The summit is the very top of a mountain.

qa.q: What is the height of Mount Everest?
qa.e: Everest's height was measured as 8,849 metres in 2020.

qa.q: Who were the first to reach the summit of Mount Everest in 1953?
qa.e: Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the top on 29 May 1953.

qa.q: Who was the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest?
qa.e: Bachendri Pal reached the summit in 1984.

qa.q: What is a 'base camp'?
qa.a: the main camp at the foot of a mountain where climbers start and rest
qa.e: Climbers gather supplies and rest at base camp before climbing.

qa.q: Why do climbers on Everest carry oxygen?
qa.a: The air at great heights has less oxygen
qa.e: Higher up, the air is thinner, so each breath has less oxygen.

qa.q: What does 'expedition' mean?
qa.a: a journey made for a special purpose
qa.e: Mountain climbs and explorations are called expeditions.

qa.q: Mount Everest lies on the border of:
qa.e: Everest is on the Nepal–China (Tibet) border.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'determine'?
qa.e: The suffix -ation turns the verb 'determine' into the noun 'determination'.

qa.q: What is the adjective formed from 'courage'?
qa.e: Courage + -ous = courageous (full of courage).

qa.q: What does 'hopeless' mean?
qa.e: The suffix -less means 'without'.

qa.q: What is the noun formed from 'achieve'?
qa.e: Achieve + -ment = achievement.

qa.q: 'When Pema first tried to climb the hill, she stopped halfway. The next morning, she tried again.' Pema is:
qa.e: She keeps trying after failing — she is determined.

qa.q: What does 'fearless' mean?
qa.e: -less means without, so fearless means having no fear.

qa.q: 'The climbers worked ___ to reach the top.'
qa.e: We need an adverb to describe how they worked: tirelessly.

qa.q: 'Every day Pema climbed a little higher. By winter, she reached the top without stopping.' What helped Pema succeed?
qa.e: She climbed a little higher every day — regular practice.

qa.q: 'Riya ___ just reached base camp.'
qa.e: Riya is singular, so we use 'has' + reached.

qa.q: 'We ___ climbed this hill many times.'
qa.e: 'We' takes 'have' in the present perfect.

qa.q: Which sentence about the 1953 climb is correct?
qa.a: Tenzing and Hillary reached the summit in 1953.
qa.e: 'In 1953' is a definite past time, so simple past is used.

qa.q: 'I have lived in Shimla ___ 2020.'
qa.e: 2020 is a point of time, so we use 'since'.

qa.q: 'The team has trained ___ three months.'
qa.e: Three months is a length of time, so we use 'for'.

qa.q: What is the past participle of 'go'?
qa.e: go – went – gone. 'Gone' goes with has/have.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?
qa.e: Has + finished (past participle) is present perfect.

qa.q: 'Have you ever ___ snow?'
qa.e: After 'have', we need the past participle: see – saw – seen.

qa.q: Which force guards India's seas?
qa.e: The Navy protects our seas and coastline.

qa.q: Who is the Supreme Commander of India's armed forces?
qa.e: The Constitution makes the President the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

qa.q: On which date is Army Day celebrated?
qa.e: Army Day is on 15 January. The other dates are Republic Day, Independence Day and Gandhi Jayanti.

qa.q: On which date is Air Force Day celebrated?
qa.e: Air Force Day is on 8 October.

qa.q: On which date is Navy Day celebrated?
qa.e: Navy Day is celebrated on 4 December.

qa.q: What does 'homage' mean?
qa.a: deep respect shown to honour someone
qa.e: To pay homage is to honour someone with respect.

qa.q: Apart from guarding the borders, soldiers also:
qa.a: help people during floods and earthquakes
qa.e: The armed forces carry out rescue and relief work during disasters.

qa.q: Which force flies fighter jets to defend India's skies?
qa.e: Defending the skies is the main job of the Air Force.

qa.q: What does 'patriotism' mean?
qa.e: Patriotism is love and loyalty for one's country.

qa.q: What does 'valour' mean?
qa.e: Valour means bravery, especially in battle.

qa.q: What is India's highest wartime gallantry award?
qa.e: The Param Vir Chakra is the highest wartime gallantry award. Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award; the Arjuna Award is for sports.

qa.q: What is India's highest peacetime gallantry award?
qa.e: The Ashoka Chakra is the highest gallantry award for bravery away from the battlefield.

qa.q: Where is the National War Memorial?
qa.e: The National War Memorial is in New Delhi, near India Gate.

qa.q: What does 'sacrifice' mean?
qa.a: giving up something precious for others
qa.e: Soldiers sacrifice comfort, time with family and sometimes their lives.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'brave'?
qa.e: Valiant means brave. The others mean fearful.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'brave'?
qa.e: Cowardly means lacking courage — the opposite of brave.

qa.q: Change to passive: 'The soldiers built the bridge.'
qa.a: The bridge was built by the soldiers.
qa.e: The object becomes the subject; past tense → was + built; add 'by the soldiers'.

qa.q: Change to passive: 'The army helps the villagers.'
qa.a: The villagers are helped by the army.
qa.e: Simple present with a plural subject → are + helped.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
qa.a: The flag was hoisted by the captain.
qa.e: The subject (the flag) receives the action, and the verb is was + hoisted.

qa.q: Change to active: 'The medal was given by the President.'
qa.e: The doer (the President) becomes the subject; 'was given' becomes 'gave'.

qa.q: 'The parade ___ watched by thousands of people.'
qa.e: 'Parade' is singular, so we use 'was' + watched.

qa.q: 'The letters were ___ by the soldiers.'
qa.e: The passive needs the past participle: write – wrote – written.

qa.q: 'The rescue boats ___ sent by the Navy.'
qa.e: 'Boats' is plural and the action is in the past, so 'were' is correct.

qa.q: Why is the passive used in 'The fort was built long ago'?
qa.a: The doer is unknown or not important
qa.e: We don't know or need to say who built the fort, so the passive fits.

qa.q: 'On Siachen's ice where the cold winds blow.' What kind of place is described?
qa.e: 'Ice' and 'cold winds' show Siachen is a frozen glacier.

qa.q: 'In Thar's hot sands where few dare go.' The Thar is a:
qa.e: The Thar is a hot, sandy desert, mostly in Rajasthan.

qa.q: The Siachen Glacier is known as:
qa.e: Soldiers guard Siachen at great heights in freezing cold.

qa.q: 'We sleep in peace, we laugh, we play — / Dear soldiers, thank you, every day.' Why can we sleep in peace?
qa.e: The poem links our peace to the soldiers 'on guard'.

qa.q: What is the tone of the poem 'Dear soldiers, thank you, every day'?
qa.e: Words like 'thank you' and 'dear' show gratitude and respect.

qa.q: 'On Siachen's ice where the cold winds blow, / In Thar's hot sands where few dare go.' Which word rhymes with 'blow'?
qa.e: 'Blow' and 'go' both end in the 'oh' sound.

qa.q: 'You stand on guard as days roll by.' What does 'as days roll by' mean?
qa.a: as time passes, day after day
qa.e: Days 'rolling by' means time passing.

qa.q: A poem written to honour and thank someone is called a:
qa.e: A tribute shows respect; a limerick is a funny poem.

qa.q: Which spelling is correct?
qa.e: The correct spelling is g-r-a-t-e-f-u-l, from the same root as 'gratitude'.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'thankful'?
qa.e: Grateful and thankful mean the same.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'grateful'?
qa.e: The prefix un- makes the opposite: ungrateful.

qa.q: What does 'appreciate' mean?
qa.a: to value something and be thankful for it
qa.e: When we appreciate someone's work, we value it.

qa.q: Which is the best line for a thank-you note?
qa.a: Thank you for the warm sweater you knitted; it keeps me cosy every morning.
qa.e: A good thank-you note says what you are thankful for and how it helped.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'grateful'?
qa.e: Gratitude is the feeling of being grateful.

qa.q: 'I am grateful ___ your kind words.'
qa.e: We are grateful FOR a thing.

qa.q: 'We are grateful ___ our soldiers for their service.'
qa.e: We are grateful TO a person.

qa.q: Which town did Rani Abbakka rule?
qa.e: Rani Abbakka ruled the port town of Ullal in coastal Karnataka.

qa.q: Rani Abbakka fought against the:
qa.e: She resisted the Portuguese, who were trying to control the western coast.

qa.q: In which century did Rani Abbakka live?
qa.e: She ruled Ullal in the 1500s, the 16th century.

qa.q: Ullal, Rani Abbakka's kingdom, is in present-day:
qa.e: Ullal is near Mangaluru in Karnataka.

qa.q: Why did the Portuguese want Ullal?
qa.a: It was a busy port for trade
qa.e: They wanted to control ports and the spice trade on the coast.

qa.q: What does the title 'Abhaya Rani' mean?
qa.e: 'Abhaya' means without fear.

qa.q: The Portuguese demanded 'tribute' from Rani Abbakka. Here 'tribute' means:
qa.a: a payment a ruler is forced to give to a stronger power
qa.e: In history, tribute is money or goods paid to a more powerful ruler. (In a poem, 'tribute' means honour — the same word with two meanings!)

qa.q: Where did Vasco da Gama land in India in 1498?
qa.e: He reached Kozhikode on the Malabar coast in 1498.

qa.q: 'When the school fair got rained out, class monitor Leela did not panic.' This shows she was:
qa.e: Not panicking means staying calm.

qa.q: 'She split the class into teams: one moved the stalls, one dried the chairs, and one made new signboards.' What did Leela do?
qa.a: She shared out the work in teams
qa.e: She split the class into teams with different jobs.

qa.q: '"A leader listens and then acts," her teacher smiled.' What does this mean?
qa.a: A good leader hears others before deciding
qa.e: Listening first helps a leader make good decisions.

qa.q: Which word names the quality of a leader?
qa.e: Leadership is the quality; leader is the person; lead is the verb.

qa.q: Which action shows good leadership?
qa.a: Making a plan and sharing tasks fairly
qa.e: Good leaders plan and treat their team fairly.

qa.q: What does 'responsibility' mean?
qa.a: a duty you are trusted to do
qa.e: When you have a responsibility, people trust you to do it.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'courageous'?
qa.e: Bold means brave — like courageous.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'leader'?
qa.e: A follower goes after a leader. Captain, guide and chief are like leaders.

qa.q: 'The Portuguese were powerful, ___ Abbakka did not surrender.'
qa.e: The second part is a surprise compared with the first, so 'but' shows the contrast.

qa.q: 'She fought bravely ___ she loved her land.'
qa.e: Loving her land is the reason she fought, so 'because' fits.

qa.q: 'The enemy ships came near, ___ the soldiers got ready.'
qa.e: Getting ready is the result of the ships coming, so 'so' fits.

qa.q: '___ she had fewer soldiers, she kept fighting.'
qa.e: Fewer soldiers and still fighting is a contrast, so 'Although' fits.

qa.q: 'Would you like tea ___ coffee?'
qa.e: 'Or' gives a choice between two things.

qa.q: Which sentence uses 'although' correctly?
qa.e: 'Although' already shows contrast, so we don't add 'but'.

qa.q: 'Wait here ___ I come back.'
qa.e: 'Until' means up to the time when I come back.

qa.q: The conjunction 'because' tells us the:
qa.e: 'Because' answers the question 'Why?'
